items.question: How do I calm down and wait on God so I can hear from Him?
items.text:
What a good question, and our books speak to it directly.

The first thing is simply to calm down. Jesus stirred up the greatest miracle by asking the agitated crowd to sit down, and the word to you is the same: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Philippians 4:6) [1]. A flustered person running from one emergency to another will not think clearly and will not hear from God, so give yourself time to calm down in His presence — sometimes it takes several days [1].

Waiting is also a skill to be learned, not just a feeling. "They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength" (Isaiah 40:31), and in Acts the Holy Spirit spoke to Paul and the prophets as they waited on God and ministered to Him [4]. You can wait with targets, giving yourself a number of hours to pray, following the example of Jesus who "continued all night in prayer" (Luke 6:12) [5]. You can also wait together with fellow ministers, as the prophets and teachers did at Antioch when "the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul" (Acts 13:1-2) [7], and with the whole congregation, as Joel 2:15-16 calls the people to a solemn assembly [7].

Silence helps too: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10) — many Christians do not hear from God because they are too busy talking, chatting or singing [2]. And some find it helps to pray in tongues while reading, since "if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful" (1 Corinthians 14:14) [5][6], or to play godly music and preaching in the background to create an atmosphere for prayer [3][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 12 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 7 of *Seeing And Hearing*, chapter 9 of *The Privilege* and chapter 24 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 46:10; Isaiah 40:31; Daniel 1:4; Joel 2:15-17; Matthew 26:40; Luke 6:12; Acts 13:1-2; 1 Corinthians 14:14; Philippians 4:6.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to pretend to be strong when I'm actually struggling?
items.text:
It's dangerous because pretending keeps you from the help you need. If your pastor knows you are weak, he can pray for you, but if you pretend to be mighty, how can he know you need help? [1][2] When you appear strong even though you are weak, nobody can help you, and you are preventing your own deliverance by covering what needs help [1][2].

The books also warn that this kind of pretending is a form of hypocrisy — appearing more committed, righteous, or spiritual than you really are, like Ananias and Sapphira, who pretended to give more than they did [8]. And there is a better way: talk about your weaknesses and personal problems rather than your achievements, and confess your sins more and more, as David did [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Duality*, chapter 11 of *Spiritual Dangers*, chapter 17 of *Now We Are At War* and chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:1-3; Numbers 16:8-10; 2 Corinthians 12:9-10.

items.question: What mistakes do pastors usually make that hurt their ministry?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
The books name several mistakes that wound a ministry. A pastor can choose to bear few fruits, leaving a fruitful place for somewhere he would rather live, when God is glorified by much fruit, as John 15:8 says [1]. He can turn into a Pharisee, caring about the chief seats and greetings in the markets, as Matthew 23:6-7 describes [2]. He can get his priorities wrong, building his own comfort instead of the church, or giving priority to the rich and powerful while setting aside the young, the children and the poor [4]. He can downplay humility and stop being childlike, when Jesus said that unless we become as little children we shall not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3) [8]. And he can be slow about ministry, not knowing what the time is, for Jesus said, "My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready" (John 7:6) [7].

There are also the quieter failures: disappointing shepherds choose the sacrifices they make instead of obeying, and they stop seeing themselves as sheep who still need leading and direction [3]. They do not remain small in their own eyes, though Saul was made head of the tribes of Israel when he was little in his own eyes (1 Samuel 15:16-17) [3]. And pride makes a man overconfident, as it did Korah, Dathan and Abiram, so that he oversteps his boundaries [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 3, 7, 8 and 9 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 31 of *The Art of Shepherding* and chapter 2 of *Not A Novice*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:16-17; Matthew 18:3; Matthew 23:6-7; John 7:6; John 15:8.

items.question: Why do people hear the same sermon differently?
items.text:
People hear the same sermon differently because, as Jesus said, "their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed" (Matthew 13:15) [1]. Some only hear your accent, some the grammar, some the stories or jokes, while others hear the principles and Scriptures, and still others hear the Spirit speaking and receive wisdom and guidance from the Holy Spirit [1].

Hearing rightly is also a matter of faith: the word preached did not profit some because it was "not being mixed with faith in them that heard it" (Hebrews 4:1-2) [8]. Judas sat at the table when Jesus spoke, yet the message did not benefit him because he did not hear with faith [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing* and chapter 16 of *Seeing And Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 4:7; Matthew 13:14-15; Luke 22:22-23; Hebrews 4:1-2.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone is using flattery or food to lead me into sin?
items.text:
Our books speak clearly about flattery, though they do not address food as a means of leading someone into sin.

Flattery is excessive praise given insincerely in order to gain favour for oneself, and it works ruin [3]. Be on guard when someone excessively praises you and your ministry, for such a person cannot be trusted; flattery is a sign of disloyalty, a mask for true intentions, and those full of effusive praises eventually leave [1]. The Scriptures warn us, "For there is no faithfulness in their mouth... they flatter with their tongue" (Psalms 5:9) [1], and Jude 16 describes such people as grumblers who speak arrogantly, "flattering people for the sake of gaining an advantage" [1]. Flattery is an injection of pride that makes you think you are what you are not, and pride goes before a fall [2]. It is one of the deadly poisons of the tongue [2][3].

As for recognizing it, you must look for the signs, for betrayal does not announce itself; if you fail to see the signs leaders are supposed to notice, you will be at the mercy of traitors [7]. A flatterer is a dangerous person, so be careful of people who flatter [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 3 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue* and chapter 97 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 5:9; Proverbs 26:28; Ecclesiastes 5:18-19; Zechariah 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:5; Jude 16.

items.question: Why is my church not growing?
items.book: Why Is This Church Not Working?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this weight, pastor. Our books name several possible reasons, and I'd gently lay them before you.

It may be that you have a low capacity for studying — people who do not study books on ministry and church growth will not have growth, and a failing church is a revelation of a lack of knowledge, wisdom and understanding [2]. It may be that you are not diligent, passive and laid-back, needing constant supervision, for pastors who make a constant effort to accomplish something are the only ones who have working churches [3]. It may be the location: you are not supposed to worship just anywhere, but in the place which the Lord shall choose (Deuteronomy 12:13-14), and perhaps it is time you relocated your church so that many more people can come [4]. It may be that you are using the wrong church growth strategy, for a house is built through wisdom and by a series of steps (Proverbs 24:3-4) [5]. And it may simply be warfare — something is fighting you, that is why your church is not growing, and pastors who are not prepared to go to war cannot have church growth [1].

Alongside these, the books also speak of a burning vision: in the absence of a burning vision for a large church you will never have real church growth [7]. And they encourage you not to be in a hurry, for the Kingdom of God is like a mustard seed (Matthew 13:31, 32) — one pastor's church began with a single member and is now a megachurch [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapters 11, 12, 17 and 18 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 1 of *Church Growth* and chapter 7 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 12:13-14; Proverbs 22:29; Proverbs 24:3-4; Proverbs 29:18; Matthew 13:31-32; Mark 6:2; 2 Timothy 2:15.

items.question: What diseases can you get from having sex before marriage?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Fornication—sexual intercourse before marriage [3][5]—opens the door to a host of diseases that come only through sexual intercourse, the STDs. Among the ten named are Gonorrhoea, Syphilis, Non-Specific Urethritis, liver diseases from Hepatitis B, Herpes Genitalis, Vaginitis, Lymphogranuloma venereum, Soft Sore (Chancroid), urinary tract infection, and cancer of the cervix, which frequent sex at an early age predisposes you to [1][2].

And it goes further than sickness: fornication brings death, for it will kill you if you acquire HIV, and unless God works a miracle you may die of AIDS [1][2]. The books also warn that a faithful partner can develop a sexually transmitted disease through no fault of their own when the other partner has sex outside the marriage [4][6]. If you wait till you marry before having sex, you may save yourself from all these diseases [1][2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers*, chapters 2 and 3 of *All About Fornication* and chapter 11 of *The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 3:15; Ephesians 5:3.

items.question: How can I know if I'm on the wrong path in life?
items.text:
The books speak to this in a few ways. One test is the company you keep: the broad way has many people on it and the narrow way has few, and it is the road with a lot of people on it that the world sees as the right road — but Jesus warned that you must be among the few who choose Him [2]. Another test is your conscience, that quiet inner voice that checks you when you go wrong; your heart has the ability to condemn you for wrongdoing, and it is only when your heart is not condemning you that you have confidence toward God (1 John 3:20-21) [4]. As you keep ignoring that voice, it becomes deadened and hardened — what Paul described as a conscience seared with a hot iron [4].

There is also the matter of proving what you are following: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:21) — every voice, prophecy, or revelation you claim to have heard from God should be subjected to the test of the Word of God and to a multitude of counsellors [3]. And remember that a way can seem right and still end in death: "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death" (Proverbs 14:12) [7]. If you have committed your way to God, as Proverbs 3:5-6 says, He is committed to directing your paths — He will block certain doors and make it impossible for you to go on certain roads [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 50 and 65 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 19, 23 and 24 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 3:5; Proverbs 14:12; Ecclesiastes 4:8; Matthew 7:13-14; John 14:4-6; Acts 24:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 3:20-21.

items.question: What should I do when one of them is a leader I trained?
items.text:
That is a painful kind of departure, and our books speak to it. When a person you trained and appointed becomes established and then leaves, plants nearby, and draws your members away, that is the presumptuous spirit Moses confronted in Korah — the arrogant assumption of privilege, speaking rudely to those above him, treating an honoured position as a small thing (Numbers 16:3, 16:8-9) [5]. It is also the pattern of Absalom, who stole the hearts of the men of Israel by sympathizing with the people and quietly belittling the king (2 Samuel 15:3, 15:6) [8].

So guard your own heart first: do not mock or gloat when such a one later falls into trouble, for "he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" (Proverbs 17:5) [2]. And be open to what God is doing in you through it, for each person who leaves can become a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Those who leave you*, chapter 4 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:3; Numbers 16:8-9; 2 Samuel 15:3; 2 Samuel 15:6; 1 Kings 11:3-4; Proverbs 17:5; 2 Corinthians 7:11; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: What does it mean to build a church on a deep foundation?
items.text:
Building a church on a deep foundation means going deeper so you can build something great for God — tall, majestic structures are only possible by going deeper [1]. Jesus told of the man who dug deep and laid his foundation on a rock, so that when the flood beat against the house it could not shake it, because it was founded on a rock (Luke 6:47-49) [1]. The deeper and stronger the foundation, the greater and taller the building [2].

That deep foundation is made of mighty foundations you must not set aside: salvation through the blood and cross of Jesus Christ; faithfulness and loyalty; evangelism and outreach; teaching the word of God and sticking to it; tithes and offerings as the source of financing for God's work; and the truth that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life [1][2]. These foundations must be protected, for "if the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (Psalm 11:3) [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Going Deeper and Doing More*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 11:3; Luke 6:47-49.

items.question: What does it mean when someone constantly accuses others and tries to control them?
items.text:
When someone constantly accuses others and tries to control them, the books describe this as witchcraft — the use of any power other than the power of God to control people. One way of establishing control is to accuse and pester someone with words, and as the accusations continue, the accuser achieves a level of control over your life, and this is witchcraft [1]. A person with a controlling spirit is a witch, and such a person wields this power through relentless accusations [2].

The books also say accusations are manifestations of hatred — your accuser is the one who hates you most [2]. And they warn that sometimes those accusing you do not even know they have moved into the realm of witchcraft [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who Accuse You*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 25:24-25; John 15:25.

items.question: What are creeping things in the spiritual sense and how do I pray against them in my church?
items.text:
Creeping things are things that sneak up on you without you realising it — spiritually, things that move upon us stealthily, so that great changes take place over a long period of time and most people hardly notice [2]. The book names four that creep upon all churches: deception, wrong attitudes like laziness, complacency and unbelief, familiarity, and the shifting of priorities, such as becoming health and educational organisations instead of missionary societies [2]. Deception is a creeping thing — the church in Europe did not degenerate overnight; the spirit of deception crept on it slowly [1][2].

As for praying against them, the book says intercessory prayer is necessary to keep out these spiritual creepers, and that intercessory prayer will fight the creeping familiarity that kills the flow of the Spirit [1]. It also says intercession deals with the law of creeping things, and points to Genesis 1:25–26, where God gave man dominion over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth [2]. Beyond that, the passages do not give a step-by-step way of praying against each of the four.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 21 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:25-26.

items.question: How do I start a new church in a town where we have no members?
items.text:
What a good question to bring, and the books speak to it plainly. You don't need a crowd to begin — two or three is enough, for where two or three are gathered in His name, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20) [6]. One pastor willing to obey God is all that is needed; the Lighthouse Cathedral began with as few as five people, and a work in Zürich began with knowing only one person [6]. If you are truly called of God, the only person you need is yourself [6].

Count the cost first, as Luke 14:28 says — sit down and count the cost before you build [5]. It will not be easy, and not many want to identify with a small thing [5]. Don't be financially desperate in these early stages; find a job and start as a lay person, so people see you are not ministering for gain [1][2]. Don't rent an expensive hall, and don't keep the church's money in your house or personal account [3][4]. The basics are praying, witnessing and following up converts [6]. Just build the church and fill it with people — pray for them, preach the Word, visit the sheep and trust God [3][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 18:20; Luke 14:28.

items.question: What does the Bible say about being a shepherd like Jesus?
items.text:
Being a shepherd is a privilege, not just a job — Jesus Himself was a shepherd, and He called Himself the Good Shepherd, as John 10:11 says [1]. When you take up shepherding, you are joining Jesus in His chosen profession, and the work involves visiting people, praying for them, counselling with the word of God, preaching and teaching [1].

A good shepherd leads his sheep, being practically available so they can see and learn from him in every area of life and ministry — anything you want your sheep to do, you must first do it yourself, as John 10:3 shows [2][7]. A good shepherd also seeks the lost: he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one lost sheep, as Luke 15:4-7 and Matthew 18:12 describe [4][8]. And the principal duty of a shepherd is to feed the flocks, so he must develop the ability to preach and teach, committing what he has heard to faithful men, as 2 Timothy 2:2 says [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Privilege*, chapters 9 and 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapter 8 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 23:1-6; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Matthew 9:36; Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:4-32; Luke 19:10; John 10:3; John 10:11; John 10:14; Ephesians 4:11 and 2 more.

items.question: How does the grace of God help my ministry reach more people and get support?
items.book: How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry
items.text:
The grace of God is what makes your gift available to many people — it is grace that brings your gift to many people, which is why some ministries have much patronage, many readers, many attenders and many supporters [1]. The grace of God also causes much support to abound towards your ministry: with great grace upon the early church, no one among them lacked, and they sold lands and houses and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:33-35) [1]. With every gift there is an accompanying grace; the apostles were gifted men, but the grace of God made their gift go even further and brought many people together to support the good work [1][3].

The grace of God also determines how far your ministry will go — it is why some pastors have larger churches and others small, why some evangelists have larger crowds, and why some have more outstanding miracles [2]. And the grace of God can be seen by the great numbers who respond to the gift of God: at Antioch a great number believed and turned to the Lord, and when Barnabas came and saw the grace of God, he was glad (Acts 11:19-24) [3]. So pray for the grace of God to work powerfully in your life and ministry [3], and be strong in that grace (2 Timothy 2:1) [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 17 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 4:33-35; Acts 11:19-24; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; 2 Timothy 2:1; Titus 2:11-12.

items.question: What is true forgiveness?
items.text:
True forgiveness is releasing all hurts, bitterness and wickedness from your heart, so that satan stares in shock at a closed door to your heart; it is to deny access to a horde of demons that are waiting [7]. In practice that means dismissing the thorny, painful issues, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, stopping resentment and anger, and cancelling all punishments you had planned [7]. As Ephesians 4:32 says, we are to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us [7].

It also means walking in love and praying for your offenders, as Jesus taught: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who despitefully use you [7]. And a test of true forgiveness is being able to pray sincerely for the well-being of the one who hurt you [1].

items.question: What happens spiritually to a Christian who commits fornication?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this. Fornication destroys your soul — as Proverbs 6:32 says, he who does it destroys his own soul — and it affects you spiritually in ways you may not fully see, gradually eroding your inner self and leading you to backslide [1][2]. With experience, the writer observed that when someone commits fornication, his spiritual life takes a nosedive and his lifestyle changes; the destruction of the soul has begun [1][2].

It is also disobedience to God, and obedience means more to Him than any sacrifice you can make — as 1 Samuel 15:22 says, "to obey is better than sacrifice" [7]. And it is a sin against your own body, for as 1 Corinthians 6:18 says, he who commits fornication sins against his own body [1][2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Spiritual Dangers* and chapter 3 of *All About Fornication*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22; Proverbs 6:32; 1 Corinthians 6:15; 1 Corinthians 6:18-19.

items.question: How do I get my life ready to die?
items.text:
What a good and sober question, and our books speak to it plainly.

Being ready to die begins with being ready to meet God, and that readiness comes only through the blood of Jesus who died for you [8]. Beyond that, readiness is a way of life: set your house in order, which is to make arrangements for the end of your life on this earth and the beginning of eternity [1]. Prepare for the gospel and preach it for the rest of your life, because what you did with the gospel and whether you served the Lord will matter so much in eternity [1]. Be ready in season and out of season, all the time, since God may need you today and not next year [3].

The books also say the only way to die the death of a righteous person is to fulfil your ministry, so that you can go out of this world in peace saying, "It is finished!" [6]. And a good general prepares for the reality of death, even making a will and an escape plan for when death strikes [5]. Paul could say, "For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain," and "I have run my race. I have finished my ministry. I have fulfilled my call. I am ready to meet my God" [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 12 of *The Preparation of the Gospel*, chapter 10 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 47 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 12:3; Amos 4:12; Malachi 3:18; Romans 1:15-16; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-18; 2 Timothy 4:2.

Please also speak with your shepherd or pastor today. Where a life may be at risk, contact emergency services or a medical professional now.

items.question: How do I get closer to God through apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. They say people do not become close to God until they accept apostles, prophets, pastors, teachers and evangelists, because these are doors for you into His presence — the writer says he grew closer to God by accepting great prophets and pastors into his life, and that you cannot go far without true apostles and prophets [1]. These men are God's gift to you, an expression of His love, as Ephesians 4:11 says, "And he gave gifts unto men: Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers" [4]. So be thankful for the servants God sends you rather than becoming discontented with them, as 1 Thessalonians 5:12 says, "appreciate those who diligently labor among you, and have charge over you in the Lord and give you instruction" [4].

At the same time, the books also tell you to judge what is said, for 1 Corinthians 14:29 says the declarations of prophets are to be assessed, and the Word of God is the standard by which we assess them [3]. A true prophet will be known by his fruits: prophets are meant to minister so that the saints are no longer children "tossed to and fro," as Ephesians 4:11,14 says, not to destabilize churches or move members about [3]. And beware of so-called prophets who do not preach the Word of God but only give personal prophecies, for anything that does not put the Word of God in its proper place is doomed to failure with the passage of time [6][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Steps to God's Presence*, chapter 18 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 7:16; 1 Corinthians 14:29; Ephesians 4:11-14; 1 Thessalonians 5:12.

items.question: How can I stay focused and really connect with God when I pray instead of getting distracted or falling asleep?
items.text:
What a real struggle this is, and you're not alone in it. One help is to build an atmosphere where you can see and hear from God while you pray — the author describes playing anointed videos and music during his prayer time, and says that when such a video is playing it is as though you are part of a miracle service during your prayer time [1]. He also warns that a cold, silent room with only polluted television left him unable to pray, so he never allowed himself to be anywhere without the ability to create that atmosphere [1].

Distractions can also be cut off deliberately. Disconnect your phone, because the telephone is a favourite tool used by the devil to interrupt your prayer, and needless interruptions break up your precious hour into piecemeal five-minute sessions [2]. Issue a "do not disturb" notice too, since you need the co-operation of the people who live with you, and they must not disturb you when you are in prayer [2].

As for sleep, watching and praying is more important than fasting and praying, and watching involves staying up at night to pray [3]. Learn to overcome sleep by going to bed early so that you can rise a great while before day — that was the life of Jesus, who rose up a great while before day and prayed (Mark 1:35) [3]. Inappropriate sleep also renders you defenceless, as when King Saul was surrounded by sleeping soldiers who were supposed to be protecting him [3]. And Jesus Himself asked, "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40) [4].

If you want to grow in praying alone, quiet time prayer will help you develop a very personal relationship with God, and each time you expand your ability to pray alone, you are expanding your ability to chalk great achievements in prayer [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Seeing And Hearing*, chapter 10 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper* and chapter 8 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:36-40; Matthew 26:42-44; Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12-13.

items.question: People are spreading lies about me in the church. How should I respond?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak directly to slander, and here is what they say.

First, know what slander does: it spreads fear and panic through a congregation, and many feel the church is collapsing because of a slanderer's words [4]. Slanderers are happy to announce the fallout from their stories [4]. But God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7) [4]. And do not worry, dear friend: God will cause you to trample over satan and his demonized slanderers, and it is only a matter of time before those slanderers burn in the very fuel they planned to use to burn down your church [4].

Second, guard your own tongue in return. A slanderer reveals secrets, but one who is trustworthy conceals a matter (Proverbs 11:13) [7]. People who fall into sin are to be helped to get up and walk again, not pushed further underground so they never rise again [7]. So don't be a destroyer; lay hands on your tongue if necessary, and make sure there is no poison in your tongue [3].

Third, the books also describe a shepherd's strong response to a wrongdoer: a pastor announced publicly that a young man was a dangerous thief and told the church to be careful of him and not believe his lies, and the sheep appreciated his strong leadership [5]. They cite "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump; purge out therefore the old leaven" (1 Corinthians 5:6, 7) [5], and "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" (Proverbs 22:10) [5]. Yet correcting the sheep does not mean disgracing them [5].

One more thing the books note: pastors are often best at slandering other pastors and helping to destroy other ministers [3], and slander from a church leader is particularly devastating because the authority of pastors gives credence to the stories they are peddling [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapter 9 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 31:11-14; Psalms 105:15; Psalms 119:21-24; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 22:10; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7; 2 Timothy 1:7; Jude 22.

items.question: Why do some Christians who give tithes prosper while others struggle?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. Tithing is a seed sown in the house of God, and everyone who sows qualifies for a harvest — "they that sow in tears shall reap in joy" (Psalm 126:5) and "give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over" (Luke 6:38) [3]. Tithing also fulfils the law of humility, since it makes you bow before your Creator and remember you did not make it on your own [5][6].

But the books also name reasons a tithe can be neutralized in a person's life: hidden sin, for "he that covereth his sins shall not prosper" (Proverbs 28:13) [1]; wrong desires, since "ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts" (James 4:2-3) [4]; strife with the brethren, for "the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace" (James 3:18) [4]; and troubled marriages, since husbands and wives are heirs together of grace "that your prayers be not hindered" (1 Peter 3:7) [1][4]. These things, the book says, fight the blessing a person invokes by tithing [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 14 and 22 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 75:6-7; Psalms 126:5; Proverbs 28:13; Matthew 6:33; Luke 6:38; James 3:18; James 4:2-3; 1 Peter 3:7.

items.question: How can a husband help his wife stay beautiful?
items.text:
A husband's care for his wife's beauty is part of loving her as his own body, for "he that loveth his wife loveth himself" (Ephesians 5:28), and it is for his own good to nourish, cherish and beautify his wife [4]. So be concerned about which dress she wears, since her beauty also depends on her dressing, and invest in her clothes—you will reap what you sow [2][3]. Tell her how you like her hair and how to do it, for a woman's long hair is a glory to her (1 Corinthians 11:15) [3], and let her always see your beautiful hair, even during sleep or sex [1].

Beauty depends on many factors—hair, dressing, make-up, even the time of day—so invest in those factors, and remember that years after the wedding Christian wives and husbands must still look attractive; pregnancy and babies are not an excuse for being careless about her looks [3]. Also let her feel loved, wanted and accepted, stay at home as often as possible, do not be harsh with her (Colossians 3:19), and listen to her a lot [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 11 and 40 of *Model Marriage* and chapter 7 of *Beauty*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:18; Ecclesiastes 9:9; Song of Songs 7:5; Song of Songs 7:7; 1 Corinthians 11:15; Ephesians 5:25-29; Colossians 3:19.

Also let her feel loved, wanted and accepted, stay at home as often as possible, do not be harsh with her (Colossians 3:19), and listen to her a lot.

items.question: What does the Bible say about wasting opportunities?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. One way people lose good opportunities is by being extravagant—living beyond your means and spending in excess is a waste of good opportunity [1]. The prodigal son "wasted his substance with riotous living" (Luke 15:11-14), and among the opportunities he wasted was the chance to benefit from his father's advice [1][2]. The same warning is given about good counsel: "Do not waste the opportunity of good advice that comes your way!" [2]

The books also name two mistakes that lead to lost opportunities: separation from God and fellowship, since the prodigal "took his journey into a far country" (Luke 15:13) [3], and greed, which can squander every great opportunity, as it did for Gehazi (2 Kings 5:27) [6]. They add that wasting what God has put in your hand means losing your position, for we will be asked to give an account of our stewardship (Luke 16:1-2) [5], and that the opportunity to win souls is not to be wasted, since a soul is worth more than the whole world (Matthew 16:26) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 4 and 10 of *Opportunities* and chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 5:27; Matthew 16:26; Luke 15:11-14; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13.

items.question: How should a church deal with sin and rebellion among its leaders?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Sin must not be trivialized or dealt with lightly; when someone has to be dismissed, he must be dismissed, and a step of judgment, rejection, dismissal, suspension or removal must be taken, otherwise the organization will begin to decline [1]. Instead of ignoring sin and wickedness and allowing evil to grow in our midst, it must receive a stiff rejection at the highest levels [1]. At the same time, God combines judgment and restoration very well when He deals with us, so we must master the art of the official rejection of sin as well as the official pardoning of sin [1].

On rebellion specifically, you must reject rebels and have nothing to do with a person who is rebelling, because if you admire a rebellious person you are in great danger of becoming a rebel yourself [2]. Rebellion is a unique sin, a specific evil distinct from every other sin [3], and Scripture compares it to witchcraft (1 Samuel 15:23) [7]. God does not need you to correct His servants; God can correct His servants without you [5]. And a person who lives continually in sin is often in rebellion against God, and that attitude of rebellion can be turned unto any of God's representatives at short notice [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 79 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapters 5 and 8 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 16:34-35; Numbers 16:41-46; Joshua 22:19; Joshua 24:19; 1 Samuel 15:23; 1 Kings 16:31; Nehemiah 9:17; Job 7:21; Job 34:37; Psalms 139:21 and 3 more.

items.question: How do I stay filled with the Holy Spirit?
items.book: The Sweet Influences of the Anointing
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say that being filled with the Spirit is stirred up in very ordinary, daily ways. Prayer meetings bring down the presence of the Holy Spirit — the early church was filled when they prayed, and "every prayer meeting brings us nearer the throne room of the Lord" [1]. Speaking to yourself in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs is the first key Paul gives in Ephesians 5:18-19, and the melody must come from the heart, not from words hastily put together [1][3]. Thankfulness is another key: "giving thanks always for all things" (Ephesians 5:18-20) opens you to be filled, while criticism and murmuring do the opposite [2][3][4]. And the last key is humility — "submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God" (Ephesians 5:18-21) [2].

You can also stir up hunger by talking and preaching about the Holy Spirit, since "blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled" (Matthew 5:6), and by asking specifically for Him, for the Father gives the Holy Spirit to them that ask Him [5]. The books also speak of flowing with Him as a real person — talking with Him, listening for His advice, recognizing His thoughts and reminders — and as wind and as water that refreshes and makes you grow [6][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 3 of *Those Who Forget* and chapters 1 and 7 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 63:1; Isaiah 58:11; Matthew 5:6; John 20:22; Acts 2:2; Acts 4:31; Ephesians 5:18-21; 2 Timothy 1:6.

items.question: What does the Bible say about pastors criticizing or attacking other pastors and ministries?
items.book: The Church Must Send or It Will End
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this, and it is a serious matter. Pastors who attack and criticize one another instead of concentrating on the work of ministry are warned that their own ministry can come to an end because of their attack on another person's ministry [2]. The most wicked and destructive statements ever heard about the Body of Christ have come from pastors—ridiculing one another privately and from their pulpits, blackening the reputation of other ministers, then mounting the pulpit on Sunday to build the Body they destroyed during the week [4]. Do not break down somebody's house in order to build yours; you will only reap what you sow [4].

The Bible says we shall know them by their fruits, and when the fruits are broken churches, destroyed ministries and deceived pastors, the Spirit of God is not at work—the devil and the flesh are on the rampage [1]. Attacking and killing your own brother is a very bad sign, and constant analysis, criticism and mockery of fellow ministers is common in the conversation of some pastors [3]. It is time to leave other ministers to God; if someone is doing something wrong, leave him to God, for God's judgment is greater than your criticism of him [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 5 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 4 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End* and chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 4:8-12; 2 Samuel 13:28; 2 Samuel 14:28.

items.question: A leader I trained for years has just left the church. How do I handle it?
items.text:
I'm sorry — that is a hard thing to carry, and the books speak to it plainly.

First, guard your own spirit. When someone leaves, it pollutes you with seeds of hurt, anger, hatred, wickedness and revenge, and you will need to pray long and hard to get free of them, or you will fall into bitterness and unforgiveness [4]. David prayed to be kept from the snares of those who do iniquity, that the wicked would fall into their own nets while he passed by safely (Psalm 141:9-10) [4].

Then act rather than delay. If someone indicates a desire to leave, it is best for them not to stay but to go immediately, because their heart has already left; a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6), and Jesus told Judas, "That thou doest, do quickly" (John 13:27) [7]. A disloyal person must be restricted, not left free to operate normally — binding a "Judas" is to restrict him, and to do otherwise is to make yourself wiser than God [2].

Do not be quick to conclude it is all your fault, nor all theirs. Sometimes your leadership style contributes to people leaving; sometimes, in spite of the most perfect strategies, people still stir up strife against you, as they did against David [4]. It may also be that the Lord allowed it because you have not continued to follow Him as at the beginning, or because you have not exerted your authority [5]. And be careful of the judgment of Job's friends — the three pastors who mocked another church's "bad leader" later had the same thing happen to them, more severely [3].

Finally, expect God to fill the gap. Sometimes the departure of a person heralds the arrival of God's choice for you; it was when Saul's heart departed that David was revealed [6]. If you are open, each person who leaves becomes a stepping stone to a higher dimension of ministry [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 3 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 11:3-4; Psalms 141:9-10; Proverbs 3:7; John 13:27; 1 Corinthians 5:6; 1 Corinthians 14:33; 2 Corinthians 7:11.

items.question: How can a pastor's wife support her husband's ministry if she's quiet and doesn't connect with people?
items.book: The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor
items.text:
The books speak directly to a quiet and effective wife. A wife who is helpful is a quiet and effective backbone to any minister, and many ministers depend on their wives for the quiet and effective help they give [2]. That help is pictured in Genesis 2:18, where God said it is not good for the man to be alone and made him a help meet for him [2].

Quietness itself is not the problem the books warn about. The warning is against being isolated and non-communicative, because you will never be made perfect without the input of others (Hebrews 11:40), and the eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of thee" (1 Corinthians 12:20-21) [5]. So a wife can be quiet and effective in the helps ministry, in prayer, or behind the scenes, without being seen or known by the general public [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Am I Good For Nothing?* and chapter 4 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:18; 1 Corinthians 12:20-21; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Hebrews 11:40.

items.question: How should I respond when people I've loved and helped turn against me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. It's a pain every shepherd meets, and our books speak to it plainly.

Don't be surprised by it. Jesus Himself was repaid with stones for His good works (John 10:32), and every leader comes face to face with ingratitude [1]. People you loved can turn and hurt you; men you trained may not remember the help they received [1]. Some whom a leader loves return that love with flatness, with hatred, with treachery [5], and some repay love by becoming adversaries, as Psalm 109:1-5 describes [4].

So don't look to people for gratitude. A leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. If you retaliate because of ingratitude, you will lose your place in the ministry; Jesus never responded to that evil spirit of ingratitude [1]. David's response was to give himself to prayer and to ask God for judgment, that those who repaid his good with evil be clothed with shame and dishonour (Psalm 35:21-26) [2][4]. And when people leave, don't struggle: sometimes it is in your eternal destiny that they be taken away and replaced, and God raises up others you would never have known otherwise [6][7]. Keep moving and keep pressing on; learn to forgive because you have been forgiven a lot [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 11 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapters 1 and 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 5 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:1-2; Psalms 35:21-26; Psalms 109:1-5; Luke 15:11-13; John 10:32; John 21:15-17; Ephesians 6:8; 1 John 2:18-19.

items.question: What does the cross mean for me as a Christian?
items.text:
The cross stands for many things, and every time you see it you are meant to be reminded of what it symbolizes [3]. It is the symbol of the death you must experience, for when Jesus told us to carry our cross He was telling us to go to a place where we would die and lose our lives, as He said in Luke 9:23 [4]. It is also the symbol of the price Christians must pay, since you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20) [1], and the symbol of the sacrifice all of us must make to serve the Lord, as Ephesians 5:2 says [5]. In the cross we also see the love of God we must emulate, for 1 John 3:16 says He laid down His life for us and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren [1], and we see obedience, since Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8) [1][5]. It is the symbol of humility and of the blood of Jesus, for through the blood of His cross all things are reconciled to Himself (Colossians 1:20) [5].

Taking up your cross is not only His cross but yours, and it releases power in your life [6]. It has power to put away sins, for as Hebrews 9:24-26 says, He appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself, and your great sacrifices for the Lord cause your sins and weaknesses to become insignificant in comparison [6]. It enables you to die to sin and live to righteousness [6], and it brings you into a new life of faith and ministry, for Paul said, "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" [2]. Through the power of the cross a Christian will not mind being the odd one out, and will not mind giving up wealth and success to pursue the humble career of a minister of the gospel [2]. The cross also takes away the curse due rebellious people, for Galatians 3:13 says Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 9:23; 1 Corinthians 6:20; Galatians 3:13; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 2:8; Colossians 1:20; Hebrews 2:9; Hebrews 9:24-26; 1 John 3:16.

items.question: How do I stop needing people's approval and praise after I preach?
items.text:
What a good and freeing question. The books speak to this directly.

Do not look to people for gratitude or approval; a leader looks to God for rewards, for "whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:8) [1]. Your rewards depend on God, not on the people you helped, so expect your rewards from Him rather than from men [1]. One minister described how he stopped expecting people to commend him after preaching, and when he decided not to look for man's approval he felt a sense of liberty, free from men and accountable to the Lord [1].

The same counsel appears elsewhere: you do not need the approval of men, so do not worry about what people think of you — just make sure God thinks highly of you, and you will become a workman who is not ashamed (2 Timothy 2:15) [2]. People may congratulate you, but it is the Lord's approval you really need [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 9 of *The Preparation of the Gospel* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: John 3:16; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 2:15-16; 2 Timothy 4:1-2.

items.question: How can I learn to pray early in the morning before my day gets busy?
items.book:
Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer
items.text:
What a good desire, pastor. The books speak directly to this. Jesus Himself rose "a great while before day" and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35), and you are invited to learn the same practice [1]. One practical help: go to bed early so that you can rise a great while before day — that was the life of Jesus [3].

It helps to see this as building a habit. Praying at dawn is very repeatable; you can do it tomorrow and every day of the year, in every season, even on your busiest days [1]. An action becomes a habit when it is repeated many times, and if you decide to develop a habit of prayer, you are developing a habit for success [5][7]. Daniel had a custom of praying three times a day (Daniel 6:10), and Jesus had the custom of going to the synagogue on the Sabbath (Luke 4:16) [5][7].

The books also give reasons this matters: praying at dawn helps you fight prayerlessness — a Christian who has not learned to rise a great while before day is most probably a prayerless believer [2] — and it makes you ready for the battles of the day, so that God lifts you up and empowers you to overcome whatever has targeted you [2]. It also brings consistency, overcoming the ups and downs most Christians experience [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*, chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 1 of *How to Pray* and chapter 8 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Matthew 26:36-40; Mark 1:34-36; Luke 4:16.

items.question: How can I pray for the sick and be a source of healing?
items.text:
You can become a source of healing simply by praying for the sick, because healing is on the heart of God and Jesus said He was anointed to heal the broken-hearted [1]. Many people are comforted when hands are laid on them [1].

Don't be afraid to step out. Every opportunity to pray for the sick is a rehearsal for greater days ahead, and you will learn to pray for the sick in the dry season and in the rainy season [2]. Fear is a spirit that keeps you from using your gifts, and the fear of praying for the sick is a real barrier to overcome [4]. Keep your prayers short, as Jesus did — He prayed brief prayers for the sick, and short prayers are very powerful [3]. You can also pray with anointing oil, for the prayer of faith shall save the sick and the Lord shall raise him up (James 5:14-15) [5].

items.question: How can I know my strengths and use them for God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. God has asked you to be strong in the grace He has given you, and whatever grace He has given you, you should flow in it [1]. Knowing your temperament helps you know your strengths and flow in them, so learn to understand yourself [1].

Each temperament carries its own grace: if you are phlegmatic, you have a grace to do the same thing repeatedly and to carry on in an unchanging environment, so be a good teacher, pastor, or headmaster and stay faithful behind your screen [1]. If you are melancholic, it is a grace from God to be talented, deep-thinking and faithful, with an eye that naturally picks out what is disorderly [1][2]. If you are choleric, recognize the grace to be a driving personality, a finisher of projects and a natural manager, and walk in that strength of leadership [2]. If you are sanguine, the grace has been given to you to be cheerful, happy and pleasant at all times and in all circumstances [2].

A true leader knows where his strength lies, and when you discover your strengths, flow in them [2][3]. Do not be a pastor because everyone is pastoring a church, or a prophet because it is the latest fad; stay in the area which makes you unique, develop it and become strong [3]. And remember, make God your strength and trust in His mercy, for when you trust in other things you become weaker (Psalm 52:6-8) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *The Determinants*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 52:6-8; Ecclesiastes 9:11; 2 Timothy 2:1; 2 Timothy 4:7.

items.question: How do I know my work for God is not a waste of time?
items.text:
What a good question to bring, pastor. Our books say plainly that working in the world is vanity, but working in the Lord is not: "your labour is not in vain in the Lord" [2]. Paul described his work as not in vain, even while Solomon called his own work vanity [2].

They also tell us that your life's work is something God has called you to, and that in it you will not labour in vain [1][2]. And doing the work itself helps you overcome your personal problems — as you minister the Word, those problems become smaller, and God has never used perfect people who have no problems [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 2 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:11; Nehemiah 4:6; Esther 4:14; Proverbs 6:10-11; Ecclesiastes 3:13; Ecclesiastes 5:10; Ecclesiastes 5:19; Luke 12:15; John 9:4; 2 Corinthians 4:7.

items.question: How can I motivate the people who follow me as a leader?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, pastor. A true leader inspires the people around him, and since human beings are emotional, you must speak in a way that inspires them to follow — put away lifeless speeches and speak from your heart, as Paul did when the people wept after he finished preaching (Acts 20:37) [3]. You cannot motivate people if you yourself are not motivated, and you cannot affect anyone's emotions unless you yourself are emotional about what you are doing [3].

You also motivate people by going first yourself: you cannot get people to pray if you do not pray yourself, and pastors who tell their members to do one thing while they do something else often do not get good results [2]. The master key to leading people anywhere is to walk the road yourself — Jesus never told his disciples to do things he himself did not do [4]. And you must believe totally in the future your leadership is creating [2].

Beyond that, make your followers love you rather than resent you: make people feel genuinely respected, since people naturally love those who respect them [1][5], and transform those who follow you into eminent, distinguished and celebrated men, as Jesus did with his apostles [1][5]. Sacrifice for them and give them a future and a hope [1]. You can also raise morale by making them think less about themselves and more about the lost, and by speaking to them to encourage them and tell them it will be well [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 79, 83, 91 and 92 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 9 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 23:15-16; Matthew 26:35; Mark 1:17; Acts 3:6; Acts 20:33-37.

items.question: What does the Bible say happens to a society that stops being thankful to God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, pastor. When people knew God but did not glorify Him or give thanks, they became vain in their imaginations and their foolish hearts were darkened, and professing themselves wise they became fools (Romans 1:21) [2][3]. Because of this unthankfulness, God gave them up — three times — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and to a debased mind, so that men and women exchanged the natural use for what is against nature (Romans 1:26-28) [1][3].

The books describe the result in strong terms: unthankfulness is a door to many evils [2], and the descent of the human race into perversion, foolishness, madness and destruction is because men are not thankful for what God has done [3]. Being unthankful is called a dangerous curse that opens people to wicked spirits [1], and in the last days men will be marked as unthankful among the terrible faults of the human race (2 Timothy 3:1-5) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 7 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 9:16-21; Romans 1:21; Romans 1:26-28; Colossians 3:15; 1 Timothy 4:3-5; 2 Timothy 3:1-5.

items.question: How do I know if I've been called by God to do His work?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this in a few ways. One sign is a supernatural desire or interest in the work of the ministry — Paul asked Timothy to look for the desire, and didn't even mention the call, because the desire is a manifestation of a divine call [4][6]. That desire may not be sensational, but it is a burden put there by God [6].

Another is that the call is specific and personal — no one else has your calling, and you must be sure you are called rather than calling yourself, since no man takes this honour unto himself (Hebrews 5:4) [2]. And your calling is no accident; it is the fulfilment of your predestination, so those who believe they are called take God's Word, their dreams, their visions, and their quiet times more seriously [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 3 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 2 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Romans 8:30; Romans 10:1; 1 Timothy 4:15; Hebrews 5:4.

items.question: How do I forgive someone who hurt me very badly?
items.text:
I'm sorry for the pain you're carrying. The books speak directly to this.

Forgiveness means releasing the hurt, bitterness, and wickedness from your heart, giving up all claims against the one who offended you, cancelling any indebtedness, making no more mention of the matter, and cancelling all punishments you have planned for them [1][3]. It is to walk in love and pray for your offender, as Jesus said: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you" [1].

One step that makes this easier is to analyse the offender — as Jesus did on the cross when He prayed, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34) [2][3]. You may realise the person was not fully aware of the implications of his action; perhaps he is sick, ignorant, or confused, and learning to make excuses for people helps you forgive [5]. Another step is to analyse your own past sins, considering yourself lest you also be tempted [5]. And remember you are equally in need of forgiveness from God, for "if you forgive men their trespasses your heavenly Father will also forgive you" (Matthew 6:14) [3].

Do not be afraid to forgive — your forgiveness is not the end of the story, for God says, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay" (Romans 12:19-20) [7]. Your duty is to forgive and God's duty is to repay [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapters 5 and 8 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 6:14; Luke 23:34; Romans 12:19-20; Ephesians 4:32; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: A member has stopped coming to church and stopped praying. How do I help them come back to God?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Staying in fellowship matters: if we walk in the light we have fellowship one with another, as 1 John 1:7 says, and if you are in the light you will go to church and fellowship with other Christians [3]. A Christian who doesn't pray is a Christian who will fall into one temptation after another until he eventually backslides, and an uncommitted Christian is a potential backslider [8]. God expects the believer to be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, planted in the house of the Lord, with a pastor to relate to, because we are like sheep who need a shepherd [8].

So keep praying for them and keep the door open. It is time to come back home, and staying in fellowship is an important key to receiving the blessings of the Lord [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *How to Pray* and chapter 7 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:133; Proverbs 7:10; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 3:22.

items.question: What happens in my life when I don't pray?
items.text:
When you do not pray, your life is directed by happenstance—chance, circumstances, good luck and bad luck—though these events are often governed by natural and spiritual forces rather than being truly random [1]. The story of Ahab, struck by an arrow drawn at random (1 Kings 22:30-35), shows that what looks like chance can be orchestrated by evil spirits [2].

Without prayer, your life is also governed by the major curses in this world—the curse on Adam, the curse on Eve, and the curse on Ham [2][4]. It is governed by the god of this world, Satan, who is called the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4) and who directs the affairs of this world into wars, conflicts, and countless sorrows [7]. And it is governed by the wickedness of men, for the whole world lieth in wickedness (1 John 5:19) [6]. Human beings take decisions that affect you—as Pilate's decision affected Jesus—and if you do not pray, the will of capricious and unreasonable men will be implemented in your life [3]. When you do not pray, you also do not intervene or modify events taking place in the spirit realm [5].

The good news in these pages is that prayer, especially for wisdom, changes the course of a person's life and delivers him from the curses directing the masses [7]. Curses are made more bearable and are defeated through prayers for wisdom, and when you get wisdom, riches, honour, and length of days arrive and overrule the curse (Proverbs 3:13-16) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to Pray* and chapter 2 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 22:30-35; Proverbs 3:13-16; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 John 5:19; Revelation 6:1-8.

items.question: How can a young person stay away from sexual sin?
items.text:
The books give several practical steps. First, respect your sexuality rather than denying it — a proper respect for youthful lusts will save you from them [3]. Be filled with the knowledge of God's will for your sexual life, which is your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality (1 Thessalonians 4:3-4) [2]. Then find your own way of staying pure: it may be God's will for you to avoid certain books or films, certain friends, or certain places, or to marry young, or to travel with your wife [2].

Practically, avoid untimely relationships — very young people should not enter into courtship, for there is a time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1) — and enter only into relationships that lead to marriage [5]. Also be visible rather than hiding: sit in the front, make sure your pastor knows your name, and do not let yourself be an unknown entity, for those who sit far away are often practicing some kind of evil [8]. And take heart: young people can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness (Romans 1:4), and can live free from sin, for God promises to put His Spirit within you and cause you to walk in His statutes [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapters 10, 13 and 24 of *Ready@20* and chapter 4 of *Spiritual Dangers*.

items.question: How do I know if I'm ready to step into a bigger role in ministry?
items.text:
Friend, the books give you some honest questions to sit with rather than a simple checklist. They ask whether you are ready to leave familiar things behind, since full-time ministry separates you from many familiar things [1], and whether you are ready to leave your own country, region or neighbourhood, because going away is a real option for anyone coming into full-time ministry [1]. They also ask whether you can bring your whole family along this road, since some spouses reject the uncertainty of it all [8].

The books also warn that readiness is proven over time, not assumed. God does not put inexperienced people into the ministry, and Scripture says a leader must not be a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6) [4]. There are levels in God's service — doing the work, having a gift, having a ministry, and occupying an office — and you prove yourself so that you can be put into an office [4]. Knowing the greatness of God's will comes by doing it, not just by reading about it, as John 7:17 says [2].

One caution the books press: many enter full-time ministry too quickly and their ministries are frustrated, and there are people in full-time ministry who should not really be there [3]. So weigh this with wisdom, not haste.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 10 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapter 14 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd* and chapter 15 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 18:19; John 7:17; Romans 11:13; Romans 12:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Timothy 3:6; 2 Timothy 4:5.

items.question: Why is the shepherd's ministry so important in the church?
items.text:
The shepherd's ministry matters because it is the shepherd, not the prophet, whose absence scatters the sheep; it is the ministry that creates the double mega missionary church, and God has prophetically destined it to save His people and let them dwell safely [1]. Ezekiel declares that God will set up shepherds to save His people [1].

It is also a principal duty of the shepherd to feed the sheep, and the authority to lead is given to those with the ability to feed [2]. Jesus told Peter three times, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17), and the principal duty of all ministry offices is to preach and teach the Word of God [2]. Alongside this, the shepherd comforts the sheep, so that every sheep can say, "Your rod and your staff comfort me" (Psalm 23:4) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church* and chapter 11 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

items.question: What habits did Jesus have that made Him great?
items.text:
Jesus had a habit of going to church regularly — the Bible says He went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16) [1][2][3]. He also had a habit of going on prayer retreats to a particular garden, a place He often went, so that even Judas knew the place, for "Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples" (John 18:1-2) [1][2][3].

The books also hold up Daniel, who prayed at specific times of the day, kneeling three times a day and giving thanks before God, "as he did aforetime" (Daniel 6:10) — it was one of the greatest secrets of his life [1][2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 9 of *The Secret* and chapter 44 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 6:10; Luke 4:16; John 18:1-2.

items.question: How can I show God that I'm thankful for everything He's done for me?
items.text:
The books say the only real way to say "thank you" is with your life — not just with songs or words you've learned, but with something genuine that comes from you [5]. One clear way is to give Him your reasonable service: to present your body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service, and to be transformed by the renewing of your mind rather than conformed to this world (Romans 12:1-2) [2][4]. It is reasonable to give Him your entire life, your youth, and your best days, since He gave His youth and His best days for you [1].

Another way is to labour more abundantly than everyone else, as Paul did — "I laboured more abundantly than they all," yet not he, but the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:10) [2]. You can also show thankfulness by being willing, fast, and complete in your obedience, since God has called you and knows you by name (Romans 8:29-30) [3]. And thank Him in everything, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you (1 Thessalonians 5:18), and give thanks always for all things to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 5:20) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks* and chapter 5 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 107:1; Romans 8:29-30; Romans 12:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:10; Ephesians 5:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:18.

items.question: Where do demons come from?
items.text:
Our books say demons are not the same as fallen angels or Satan; they are a separate set of creatures Jesus dealt with, called *diamonion*, while the devil comes from *diabolos* [2]. They teach that demons originated from the death of the "para-humans" — the hybrid offspring produced when fallen angels had intercourse with women, the giants and tyrants of old [1]. When those half-human, half-angel beings died, their spirits could not go to heaven or hell like a human soul, so they were confined to the earth and roam about as demons [2]. As the book of Enoch puts it, "the spirits of the giants afflict, oppress, destroy, attack, war, destroy, and cause trouble on the earth" [7], and Jude 1:6 speaks of the angels who kept not their first estate being reserved in everlasting chains under darkness [1].

One of our books also describes another kind of unclean spirit: animal spirits, said to have been created by fallen angels having intercourse with animals, whose offspring continued to interbreed, producing the strange wicked spirit-animal creatures known as "unclean (animal) spirits" [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 15 and 17 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Jude 6.

items.question: How can I become a friend of God like Abraham was?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for. Our books say that Abraham was called a friend of God, and they show how he came to be one: he obeyed God even to the point of sacrificing his own son, and that obedience was the test of his love [2][4]. As James 2:23 is cited, Abraham became a friend of God by being willing to sacrifice his only son [3].

So the path they describe is obedience and sacrifice. If you love the Lord, you will obey Him no matter what it costs you [2]. God asked Abraham to give up his only son, and Abraham was completely sold out to God, with no third party between him and God [2]. They also warn that anything that becomes too precious to you can become an idol, and God may ask for it, for our God is a jealous God [5][7]. Before God could trust Abraham with great blessing, He had to be sure the blessing would never replace his love for God [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 11 of *If You Love The Lord*, chapter 12 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 13:1-3; Isaiah 41:8; Daniel 8:11-13; John 12:24; Romans 12:1-2; 2 Corinthians 8:24; James 2:23; 1 John 5:21.

items.question: How should I keep the Sabbath day as a Christian?
items.text:
The books speak to this plainly. The Sabbath is a day for going to church and hearing the word of God — Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath as His custom, and Paul went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day [1][7]. It is God-time, not family time or a day for sport, shopping, or chores [1]. It is also a day of rest: "Faith loves rest," and not keeping the Sabbath and not resting is a manifestation of faithlessness, for "he that believeth shall not make haste" [4]. The Sabbath is a sign between God and His people, a day to be kept holy — meaning special for a purpose [3][8].

There is also a word here about which day. One passage says the Sabbath day is a day of rest "whether Saturday, Sunday or Monday," and that you should not worry about which day of the week it is, only that you have chosen a day to set apart for God and rest from secular work [7]. Another passage ties the Sabbath to the seventh day and to the sign given to Israel [3][5]. Both are presented in the books.

And on the question of what is lawful, Jesus asked, "Is it lawful to do well on the Sabbath day?" (Luke 14:3), and Matthew 12:12 says it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days — the donkey was considered worthy of deliverance and healing on the Sabbath, so how much more a human being [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Seven Great Principles*, chapter 25 of *Stir It Up*, chapter 72 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 4 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 16:23; Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:2; Leviticus 23:27-32; Ezekiel 20:21; Matthew 12:12; Luke 14:3; Acts 13:14-16; Acts 13:42-45; Hebrews 4:3.

items.question: How can I have a closer relationship with God?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the heart of it is drawing near to Him personally. "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (James 4:8), and the way you do that is not in public — not at church services, conventions, or crusades — but through a regular daily quiet time, where you can know God personally rather than just knowing about Him [1][3][5][7]. It is up to you to draw near to Him on a daily basis; He will not come to you first to develop the relationship [3][7].

When you are alone with someone, you become close and intimate, you develop a bond not easily acquired in public, you acquire knowledge you cannot get in public, and you can receive a private impartation — so being alone with God is where that closeness grows [8]. One caution the books give: as you get closer to God, you may sense your own unworthiness and sin, and to love Him properly you must overcome that inferiority complex by accepting that you are forgiven and that the past is washed away by the blood of Jesus [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 6 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapter 5 of *The Secret* and chapter 21 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 27:33-36; Ephesians 4:3; Philippians 3:10; James 4:8; 1 John 1:1-2.

items.question: How can a husband and wife make love in a way that is enjoyable for both of them?
items.text:
What a good thing to want for each other. Your books say sex was created by God as something beautiful and pleasurable to be enjoyed by both husband and wife, not just for procreation [1], and that it is an art to be learned and developed, about having fun with your partner and showing care rather than scoring 10 out of 10 for performance [5].

So decide together to make it pleasurable, with both of you setting out to give and derive maximum excitement [1]. Be nice to each other during the day with small thoughtful acts, look nice and smell nice, and choose a place and lighting that suit you both [1]. Let foreplay begin with endearing conversation, loving pats, hugs and kisses [1], and keep stimulating each other during the act by holding tightly, caressing and kissing [4]. Talk to each other and express your feelings during the act, and let your partner know which movements stimulate you or distract you [1][4]. Remember that a woman's arousal builds slowly, like an electric iron heating up, while a man's is like a bulb switching on [1][4] — so the husband should continue kissing and caressing her until she is sexually excited [1]. Kissing matters too: it is an important form of intimacy, and kissing whilst making love is exciting, as Song of Solomon 1:2 says [3]. And let your partner feel that he or she has done something wonderful to you [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 28, 31 and 38 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 5:19; Song of Songs 1:2.

items.question: How can I pray like Jesus did?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. Our books hold up Jesus' own prayer life as the pattern.

There are times to pray short and powerful prayers, as Jesus did at Lazarus' tomb, believing God has heard you and then acting boldly [1][5]. But there are also times for long prayer: Jesus went out to a mountain and continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12), and rose a great while before day to pray in a solitary place (Mark 1:35) [1][5]. Develop the art of praying for several hours — start with one hour, graduate to three, then five and seven [1][5]. You can stay on the same topic for hours; it is not useless repetition, it is praying like Jesus did [1][2][3].

He also prayed with strong crying and tears (Hebrews 5:7), so loud prayer is a dimension to enter, though not every time — much prayer is quiet [2][3]. And thanksgiving is a powerful prayer: in everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you (1 Thessalonians 5:18) [2][3]. Jesus prayed all night before choosing His disciples, three hours in Gethsemane, and forty days in the wilderness; these examples should guide your prayer life [4][7]. Some set themselves targets of hours, even ten, twenty, forty or fifty hours [7]. And pray to your heavenly Father, not to anyone else, for whatsoever you ask the Father in His name He will give you (John 16:23) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 6 of *100% Answered Prayer*, chapters 1 and 7 of *How to Pray* and chapter 24 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 26:39-40; Matthew 26:42-44; Mark 1:35; Luke 1:38; Luke 6:12; John 11:41-42; John 16:23; 1 Thessalonians 5:18; Hebrews 5:7.
