items.question: How can my wife and I build a strong marriage?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. The books say a happy home does not just happen; it must be developed, and nothing happens by chance [7]. So let me give you what they give.

Build your marriage around Christ as the foundation and head of the home, for when God is the focus of both of you, you draw closer to each other because your closeness to God draws you together [7]. The Word of God is your manual for marriage, and you should build your marriage around the church, attending services and being involved together [2][3]. Develop family worship, holding quiet times together or, when that is not possible, each doing it regularly, and by all means find time to do it together, especially with the children [2][3].

Think as a Christian spouse: do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility consider others better than yourselves (Philippians 2:3), reconciling the plans you each held before marriage to suit the home, being willing to give up certain interests and preferences for its sake, and not always insisting on your own way [3]. And be the best of friends, speaking the truth in love to one another, which makes you grow up in Christ (Ephesians 4:15) and draws you closer to each other [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 7 and 9 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 32:17-20; Psalms 1:1-6; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 18:21; Proverbs 24:3; Luke 6:47-48; Ephesians 4:15; Philippians 2:3.

items.question: What does it mean if God rewards my faithfulness with more work instead of rest?
items.book: WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work
items.text:
It means God has seen your faithfulness and is entrusting you with more, not less. The reward for hard work with the least is to be given more work with much, as Luke 16:10 says, "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much" [5]. God has seen all your faithfulness in secular things and is rewarding you with more work in the ministry [1][3].

Rest is also a reward for hard work — "they may rest from their labours" (Revelation 14:12-13) — but this book reveals that God does not only give rest, but actually gives more work after the period of rest [2]. So do not expect to retire if you are God's servant; the reward for building a church is to be given even more things to build for God [8]. The reward for good pastoral work is more pastoral work, and the reward for a hard-fought ministry is more ministry [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 2 and 5 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 16:27; Luke 16:10-12; 1 Timothy 5:17-18; Hebrews 11:6.

items.question: How can I grow and be more successful without becoming overconfident and setting myself up for a fall?
items.text:
What a good and sober question, pastor. The books speak to this directly.

Growth and success are good, but the danger is that past successes feed you with confidence, so that you feel what lies ahead will be defeated as easily as what you just conquered — that is hubris born of success, and it leads to reckless advancing and defeat [4]. So let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12); if you regard yourself or your position as foolproof, you are in danger of backsliding, especially after promotion or being used by God in the past [2]. Where you are overconfident is where you can be weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2].

The safeguard the books hold out is humility, which keeps you learning. Ministers stop learning at the rate at which they become proud, unable to receive from people they despise, and so they plateau [3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, not your own strength [2], and when you are humble like a child you copy good things easily and keep growing [3]. Faith for strength and courage comes from meditating on the Word day and night (Joshua 1:8) [5], and a spiritual ambition to be useful in God's house will keep you pressing forward rather than resting on past exploits [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 7 of *Backsliding*, chapter 2 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 72 of *A Good General* and chapter 35 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 14:40-45; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: How can I know the real number of people attending our church instead of just guessing?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly. The most reliable figure is what they call Type 1 Counting — the number of people physically present, counting actual heads, because "there can be no variation in the method of counting heads who are actually present" [8]. They warn against the other kinds: estimating by how full the building looks, since a hall that seats three thousand can look full with only two thousand present [1][8]; rough estimates, which can be accurate but are sometimes totally misleading [1]; cumulative counts over several nights, which are often misleading [8]; and wild guessing [1].

They also urge you to keep real, accurate data rather than vague answers — registering members with a simple form and the key fields of names, ages, gender, telephone numbers and addresses [6]. And they say the truth is worth facing: "If you cannot tell yourself the truth, you cannot be a good leader," and knowing the actual number of souls you minister to will motivate you to work harder [2], as John 8:32 says, the truth will make you free [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *The Mega Church*, chapter 45 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 13 of *Church Growth*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 13:23; John 8:32.

items.question: There is a woman in our church who manipulates and controls people. How do I deal with her?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Our books speak directly to this. A Jezebel is not to be allowed to operate freely in the church; Scripture says, "I have a few things against you because you allowed that woman Jezebel" (Revelation 2:20), and it angers God when she is left unchecked [7]. It takes the collective rebuke of church leadership to deal with a Jezebel — one person crying foul will not correct or control her [3]. God wants more people to identify the Jezebels in our midst and stop them [3].

Be aware that she may present as spiritual, even as a prophetess and a teacher of the Word, and that spirituality is found in the most evil of persons [6]. She is also a mistress of seduction and persuasion — gentle, sweet and seductive, so that it does not occur to anyone they are being charmed and convinced [3]. If she is allowed to go uncorrected, you may lose everything, just as Elijah lost his ministry [7]. One man of God confessed that failing to confront the Jezebel in their midst cost him his life, his job, his church and his career — twenty-five years of work [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 4, 10 and 21 of *Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order* and chapter 15 of *Can’t You Do
Just a Little Bit More?*.

Scriptures referenced: Revelation 2:20.

items.question: What will heaven and the new earth be like?
items.book: Who Is He That Overcometh the World
items.text:
What a hope we have, pastor. The books describe a new heaven and a new earth where the first heaven and first earth have passed away, and there is no more sea [1][2]. God Himself will dwell with His people, and He will wipe away all tears from their eyes; there will be no more death, sorrow, crying, or pain, for the former things are passed away [1][3]. There will be no more curse, and the throne of God and of the Lamb will be there, and His servants shall serve Him [3][4][5].

It is also a beautiful city, the New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband [1][4]. A pure river of water of life proceeds out of the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life bears twelve kinds of fruit and yields its fruit every month, with leaves for the healing of the nations [4][5]. No evil thing, no abomination, and no liar can enter it, and there will be no night there, nor any need of a candle or the sun [4]. The kingdoms of this world will become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign for ever and ever [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Who Is He That Overcometh the World*, chapter 31 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 20 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

Scriptures referenced: Luke 4:6; Ephesians 1:21; 1 John 2:17; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 21:1-5; Revelation 22:1-5.

items.question: How can churches grow in poor areas if they can't afford to pay pastors and workers?
items.book: Laikos Lay People and the Ministry
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. The key is the lay or tent ministry—pastors and evangelists who labour without being paid, as Paul did when he worked as a tent maker alongside Aquila and Priscilla [1][2]. Most of the ripened harvest fields are in the poor regions of the world, and the ministry of unpaid pastors and evangelists is the key to continued church planting there [1][2].

So the counsel is practical: find a job and start or pastor the church as a lay person, rather than becoming financially dependent on a small congregation for your survival [5][6]. When people see you are not ministering for financial gain, they will be more interested in your new church [5][6]. And lay people can do far more than give money—doctors, teachers, accountants, and many others can become fruitful lay pastors, so that long lists of pastors are people the church does not have to pay [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*, chapters 9 and 20 of *Church Planting*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 3 of *Church Growth*.

items.question: What does it mean to be called by God?
items.text:
To be called by God is a far greater privilege than any earthly appointment, and it means several things together. It means you have been summoned distinctly — identified, called out by name and selected by God, as He did with Moses, Bezaleel, Samuel, Zacchaeus and many of the disciples [1]. It means you have been separated for His purposes, distinguished and kept apart from others by a boundary, as the Lord separated the tribe of Levi to bear the ark and minister before Him [2][7]. It also means you have been appointed by God for a special purpose, given a charge and set over something [5], and that you have received an office from the Lord with its responsibilities and authority [3].

Along with that, being called means you have received special mercy from the Lord — His compassion and forbearance, so that after salvation the call is His greatest act of forgiveness and kindness [5]. It means you have received a gift from God, a natural capacity freely given, which is why those called seem to do certain things effortlessly [4]. It means you have received a ministry from God, coming into the duties and functions of a particular stream of Kingdom work [8], and that you are sent out — dispatched on a journey to serve Him, often sent away from family and friends [7]. And your calling is according to God's own purpose and grace, given us in Christ Jesus before the world began (2 Timothy 1:9), so it is important not only to obey the call but to find out the purpose for which God called you [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 1 of *Predestination*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 29:1; Deuteronomy 10:8; Deuteronomy 32:8; 1 Chronicles 15:16-19; 1 Chronicles 23:13; Mark 1:19-20; Luke 2:40; John 1:14; Acts 13:2; Romans 1:1 and 10 more.

items.question: What should someone who just gave their life to Christ learn first?
items.text:
What a joy to hear of someone newly born again. The first thing to understand is that this is not merely joining another religion — it is the experience of a great change in your life, a spiritual heart transplant, and you need understanding of what has happened to you so you can grow in grace [7].

They should also be taught the elementary principles of the faith, for anyone who comes to Christ will have to be taught these, and the way you are taught the elementary principles of Christ permanently determines your spiritual make-up [2]. And they must never forget the person who led them to Christ, for that one is the most special person in their life — their greatest treasure is their salvation, and it came through the toil and effort of dedicated Christians [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those Who Forget* and chapter 1 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 21:34-36; 1 Corinthians 4:15; Hebrews 5:12.

items.question: Why is it dangerous to think you're untouchable or indispensable in ministry?
items.text:
Thinking you are untouchable is the very mindset of a dangerous person: "My father cannot sack me, my father cannot discipline me, my father cannot deal with me" [1]. Absalom felt he could not be sacked or transferred away, and that same spirit is seen in a senior associate who believed the word "transfer" should never be applied to someone of his rank [1]. As soon as you begin to think of yourself as indispensable, you are becoming proud and deceived, and pride always comes before a fall [1].

The danger is real, because God is not bound to keep using you as you are. Do not think that you are indispensable; if you do not do what God wants you to do, your ministry will be taken away from you and given to another, as Luke 19:24 says, "Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds" [2]. And a true Absalom is not corrected by punishment or years of hard discipline; two years of exile and difficulty did not change his heart, he only became hardened and more dangerous [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons* and chapter 6 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 14:32; Luke 19:24; Romans 11:29.

items.question: What happens when you pray for wisdom?
items.book: Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry
items.text:
When you pray for wisdom, God gives it generously to those who ask — as James 1:5 says, if you lack wisdom, ask of God, who gives liberally and does not upbraid [6]. Solomon is the great example: he asked for an understanding heart to judge God's people, and the request pleased the Lord [6].

The books describe several effects. Praying for wisdom gives you a large heart — a great depth of understanding and insight [5]. It makes your wisdom excel the wisdom prevailing in your nation, as Solomon's excelled the wisdom of the East and of Egypt (1 Kings 4:30) [1][5]. It makes you wiser than your contemporaries, as Solomon was wiser than all men (1 Kings 4:31) [1]. It makes you a man of proverbs and songs (1 Kings 4:32) [1], and it makes you appreciate nature — the trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things and fishes (1 Kings 4:33) [2]. It also causes people to travel from afar to hear the wisdom God has given you, and causes kings and great men to pay attention to your wisdom (1 Kings 4:34), for by wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15) [3].

Beyond that, wisdom makes curses more bearable and overrules their effect — when you get wisdom, riches, honour, length of days and many blessings arrive in your life (Proverbs 3:13-16) [4]. Women are helped by wisdom, delivered from blindly following men, and through wisdom, which is medical science, childbearing is not as destructive [4][8]. And the black man who has historically been at the bottom rises through the gift of wisdom, no longer the lowest and least when he walks in the wisdom of God [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 26 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry* and chapter 3 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 3:9-11; 1 Kings 4:29-34; Proverbs 3:13-16; Proverbs 8:15; Luke 11:13; 2 Corinthians 4:4; James 1:5.

items.question: How can I avoid becoming too familiar with my leaders or with people I look up to?
items.book: Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar
items.text:
What a good question to ask, and the books speak to it plainly. The heart of it is this: familiarity means knowing someone so well that you lose your admiration, respect and sense of awe, becoming presumptuous and too confident in a way that shows a lack of respect [6]. So guard your heart against despising the anointed simply because you see their ordinariness — as Psalm 41:9 says, "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me" [2].

Practically, be quick to detect subtle indications of familiarity, and remember that a subordinate is not qualified to direct or correct his leader — Peter thought his friendship with Christ gave him the authority to rebuke Jesus, and Jesus cut him down to size urgently, calling him "Satan" (Matthew 16:23) [3][8]. Watch the groups prone to it: those who frequently interact with the leader, those who know too much about him, his friends, and those who have been promoted [4][5]. It takes spiritual discipline not to become familiar, and a leader should keep a degree of mystique around him [6][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*, chapter 95 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapters 8 and 10 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar* and chapter 13 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 41:9; Song of Songs 8:6; Matthew 16:15-17; Matthew 16:22-23; Mark 6:2-3; Mark 6:5; John 6:10-11.

items.question: What does the anointing do for someone's ministry?
items.text:
The anointing brings supernatural help for your life and ministry, just as David said, "I have given help to one who is mighty" (Psalm 89:19b) [1][5]. It raises you up to heights in ministry and establishes you, for God said, "With My holy oil I have anointed him. With whom My hand will be established" (Psalm 89:20-21) [1]. It also introduces strength to your ministry, so that even your arm will be strengthened (Psalm 89:21) [1].

It protects you from deception and the blind spots that plague ministers, the very thing Jesus rebuked when He said, "You blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel!" (Matthew 23:24) [1]. The anointing enables you to build and restore, to lay brick upon brick and raise up foundations [2], and it sets the bound free, for logical teaching cannot open prison doors—it is by the anointing that freedom comes [4]. It comforts those who mourn (Isaiah 61:2) and restores beauty and attractiveness, so that people are drawn to an anointed person without knowing why [4]. It reaches beyond your own country and nation (Isaiah 61:5) [2], and it gives you a long-lasting ministry, for "his seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before me" (Psalm 89:36-37) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 15 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 89:19-21; Psalms 89:29; Psalms 89:36-37; Isaiah 61:2-3; Isaiah 61:5-6; Matthew 23:24.

items.question: What does the Bible say about the importance of skill for getting things built?
items.text:
Yes, friend, our books speak to this directly. Skill is the master key to building, and failure to build reveals a lack of practical skills — impractical men build nothing [1][2]. Solomon himself acknowledged he had no one who could skill to hew timber like the Sidonians, and he hired skilled workers for the house of the Lord (2 Chronicles 2:7-8) [1].

Skill also determines who is chosen and how far you rise: Daniel and his friends were found ten times better than all the magicians because God gave them knowledge and skill (Daniel 1:17-20) [2]. And building itself reveals that you are prudent and practical, like the five wise virgins who made practical arrangements for extra oil (Matthew 25:1-2) [3]. One caution our books give: it is not by education or human power that the Church is built, but by the Spirit — "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6) [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Determinants*, chapter 64 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 3 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 9:25-26; 2 Chronicles 2:7-8; Ecclesiastes 2:4-6; Ecclesiastes 9:11; Daniel 1:17-20; Zechariah 4:6; Matthew 25:1-2.

items.question: How should a Christian live simply and avoid wasting money?
items.text:
What a good and honest question. Our books speak to this plainly.

If you waste what God has put into your hand, you will lose your valued and privileged position, and God will one day ask you to give an account of your stewardship, as the steward in Luke 16:1-2 was called to account [1]. Wasters tend to become poor, while those who halt the wastage tend to become rich [1]. So cut out waste — most poor nations waste half their resources, and that is why they remain poor [6]. Do not have an expensive lifestyle; cut your coat according to your size, and avoid grandiose and expensive things others may be doing [6]. Develop a dislike for loans and gifts, for every admirer of gifts and loans is likely to fail in leadership, and many do not pay back their loans [6]. Learn to do things yourself, with your own hands, rather than sitting aloof as though you were an executive when you are not [6].

Watch your company too, for the prodigal wasted his substance with harlots (Luke 15:25), and evil company corrupts good habits (1 Corinthians 15:33) [3]. And beware of get-rich-quick schemes; wise businessmen are wary of them, and the Kingdom is like a mustard seed that needs time to grow — there are no short cuts in Christianity [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 2 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 30:3-6; Psalms 27:4; Luke 15:12-14; Luke 15:25; Luke 16:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:33.

items.question: How did Paul become equal to or greater than Peter as an apostle?
items.text:
The books say Paul caught up with and even overtook those who were ahead of him through wisdom — Peter himself acknowledged that Paul wrote "according to the wisdom given unto him" (2 Peter 3:14-16), and that catching-up wisdom has two parts: walking in the grace of God and working harder than those ahead of you [6]. Paul said, "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10) [2], and he was bold to say he was "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5) [1][3]. He also became a man of abundant revelations, and the book says promotion in ministry comes through an abundance of revelations, which come through books [5].

There is also a sober thread here: the book says that although Peter was forgiven, there was a sense in which Jesus' glory and power lifted from Peter's ministry after the crucifixion, and another, Paul, rose up and took the pre-eminence in the church [1][2]. Paul saw himself as a replacement, "one born out of due time," the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:8-9) [3]. And yet the same books caution that the words of Jesus are on a different level from the words of Paul — Paul was a sinner saved by Christ, a servant, not the second son of God, and Jesus' words must be taken more seriously than what Paul or Peter said [4][7][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 13 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*, chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*, chapter 7 of *WOM13. The Big Secret - Your Ministry Depends on Books*, chapter 13 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry* and chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 34:7; Numbers 5:20-22; Matthew 18:1; Matthew 18:4; 1 Corinthians 15:8-10; 2 Corinthians 11:5; 2 Corinthians 12:7; 2 Corinthians 12:11-12; 2 Peter 3:14-16.

items.question: What does it mean to make a C-turn toward Jesus instead of a U-turn away from him?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
A C-turn is a swerve to the side — not a reversal, but a manoeuvre that takes you off the wrong course onto a better way [2]. Andrew and John show this: they had been disciples of John the Baptist, and when John pointed out the Lamb of God, they did not turn away from the ministry but turned deeper and further into God, following Jesus (John 1:35-37) [1]. Peter likewise swerved off the fisherman's road into full-time ministry when Jesus said, "Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men," and immediately he left his nets (Matthew 4:18-20) [3].

The book also warns against being too stiff or insistent on your original plan, since that can get you into big trouble; you must be flexible and capable of C-turns [3]. Jesus Himself made a C-turn, moving away from the country of the Gadarenes when the people asked Him to leave (Luke 8:37), yet He did not stop His ministry of casting out devils and healing — He simply shifted to where He was more welcome [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 4:18-20; Luke 8:37; John 1:35-37.

items.question: What does it mean to be a person of faith?
items.text:
Being a person of faith is closely tied to obedience: faith is equated with obedience, and an obedient person is a man of faith — obeying God is the exercising of your faith [1]. When you do not believe, you are disobedient [1].

It also shows up in your attitude, since your attitude is a clear revelation of your faith and beliefs, and to have faith in God means to have a good attitude [2]. And it takes great faith to carry on in prayer, so anyone who persists in prayer is a man of faith [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 10 of *Faith Secrets* and chapter 5 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 9:22-23; Hebrews 11:1.

items.question: How do I become anointed by the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Friend, our books say plainly that the anointing is the Holy Spirit Himself, and that God decides who becomes anointed — no matter how hard you work or follow principles, He divinely chooses whom He will allow to come close to Him [8]. So you must ask before it shall be given, seek before you find, and knock before the door is opened [8].

That said, the books also describe steps along the way. You need to be led by the Holy Spirit, for your destiny is to become an anointed person [4]; and you must become someone who can follow Him even when He leads you against your natural inclinations, as Jesus was led into the wilderness [1]. Waiting on God is an important step — as Isaiah 40:31 promises, those who wait on the LORD gain new strength and mount up with wings like eagles [2]. And the anointing comes where there is unity, not strife: the apostles were all with one accord in one place before the Spirit fell, as Acts 2:1 records [2].

The books also speak of receiving the Spirit by the hearing of faith — soaking in messages on the anointing until you are saturated, as one man listened to Kenneth Hagin for ten years before he received the anointing to teach [3]. And you can flow with the Holy Spirit as a real person, talking with Him, listening for His advice, and recognizing His gentle pressures [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5 and 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*, chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 1 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 28:1; Isaiah 40:31; Isaiah 45:15; Matthew 4:1; Luke 4:1-15; John 20:22; Acts 1:4; Acts 2:1-2.

items.question: Different topic: how do I pray effectively?
items.text:
On praying effectively, the books say to learn to pray all day and all night long, and you will experience one hundred per cent answers to your prayers; there are times you need to spend many hours in prayer [8]. If Jesus had to pray for long hours, then you will also have to, and you can pray on the same topic for hours — Jesus did it, and it is not useless repetition [8].

There is also a dimension of loud prayer: Jesus offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, as Hebrews 5:7 says, and so can you [8]. That said, you need not always shout — most of the time you cannot hear this author when he is praying, because he usually prays very quietly, but there are times he prays with strong cries and tears [8]. And God wants us to give thanks: in every thing give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you, as 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says, and as you thank Him you will experience many breakthroughs [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *How to Pray*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Thessalonians 5:18; Hebrews 5:7.

items.question: How can I grow spiritually and bear fruit as a Christian?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. Our books speak to this directly.

First, growth itself is the aim: after you are born again, your main aim must be to grow, moving from childhood to adulthood and from immaturity to maturity, because a Christian without converts is immature [1]. Maturity matters because when you are spiritually mature you are dominated by the Spirit, and the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance — becomes evident, as Galatians 5:22-25 says [6].

Practically, the books name several obstacles to overcome: spiritual sicknesses like laziness, pride, and living in sin, since nothing affects fruitful Christian living like sin does, and we are told in 2 Peter 1:5-8 to add to our faith virtue, temperance, patience, godliness, kindness and charity, for these make you neither barren nor unfruitful [2]. You must also overcome instability — abide in Christ, for as John 15:4, 5 says, the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide, and a tree often transplanted will never reach its fruit-bearing potential [4]; those planted in the house of the LORD shall still bring forth fruit in old age, as Psalm 92:13, 14 says [3]. And you must overcome inactivity, for passive Christians bear no fruits — witnessing, teaching, and helping in the church will get you active in the things of God [3].

Alongside that, have spiritual goals and great ambitions to do something for God, being fruitful in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God, as Colossians 1:10 says, forgetting what is behind and pressing toward the mark as Philippians 3:13, 14 says [5]. And know that God has linked answered prayer to fruit bearing: He chose and ordained you that you should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain, that whatsoever you ask of the Father in His name He may give you, as John 15:16 says [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Many Are Called*, chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 6 of *Seven Great Principles* and chapter 3 of *100% Answered Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 92:13-14; John 15:4-5; John 15:16; 1 Corinthians 13:11; Galatians 5:22-25; Philippians 3:13-14; Colossians 1:10; James 5:16; 2 Peter 1:5-8.

items.question: How can a young person deal with sexual desires and stay pure?
items.text:
The books speak to this directly, and the first thing they say is to respect those desires rather than deny them. "A proper respect for youthful lusts, rather than a denial of them will save you from them" [4]. Lust is an animal desire for sexual indulgence, and if you do not respect these instincts they will overwhelm you and lead you away from God's plan for your life [2]. Desires are real forces, and they are peculiar to the young — Ecclesiastes 12:5 says "desire shall fail" in old age [5].

The command itself is to flee: "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (2 Timothy 2:22) [2][5]. Joseph is the example — he was about eighteen when Potiphar's wife tried to have sex with him, and he lived free of fornication, immorality and lasciviousness [1]. You are told to keep yourself from influences that steal you away from the influence of the Holy Spirit, and Revelation 14:4 shows that those not defiled are able to follow the Lamb wherever He goes [2].

There is also hope, not just warning. Holiness is engineered by the Spirit of holiness, not by being older — age has nothing to do with holiness, and every young person can be empowered by the Spirit of holiness [7]. God promises, "I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes" (Ezekiel 36:27) [7]. And the will of God is clear: 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4 says your sanctification is that you abstain from sexual immorality, so make that one of your clearest and most energetic goals, finding the particular way God would have you keep yourself from fornication [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 10, 12, 13 and 20 of *Ready@20* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 41:46; Ecclesiastes 12:5; John 8:46; Romans 1:4; Ephesians 5:5-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:3-4; 1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 2:22; Revelation 14:4.

items.question: Why should we not boast about our own strength or willpower when we survive something?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. When people credited a man's survival to his resilience and strong willpower, he died of a heart attack a week later, and the question was asked, "Where was his strong will power?" [1]. God does not like it when you boast about things He has given you as though you did not receive them, as 1 Corinthians 4:7 says: "What hast thou that thou didst not receive?" [1].

When a Christian keeps boasting about his strength, Satan hears him and decides to test him; where you are over-confident is where you can be weakest, because you have dropped your guard [2][3]. Staying on the right track is largely by the grace of God, not by your own strength, so "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12) [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 12 of *Those who are Proud*, chapter 3 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 5 of *Backsliding*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 1:20; 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 10:12.

items.question: How should a pastor plan church finances when people don't pay the money they pledged?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. A wise pastor should not expect more than 30% of pledges to come in, and must never budget on what the congregation has pledged, because most members will not pay what they promised [1][2][3][4]. Pastors who budget on promised amounts are usually accused of misusing funds, since the full amounts are never realized [1][2].

So plan on the regular tithes and offerings as your main source of project financing, and see fund-raising as only a boost to what you already have [1][2][6]. It is wise to save toward a project before you even begin fund-raising, so the work goes on whether people pay up or not [1][2]. And when you do take pledges, keep the payment period short — one week to three months — because a few days after making them, many Christians forget the promises they made in church [2][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12 and 14 of *Church Growth* and chapters 2 and 6 of *Church Administration*.

Scriptures referenced: Titus 1:5.
items.label: answerable

items.question: How can we grow our church like the early church did?
items.text:
The early church grew as the apostles preached the word and the Lord added to the church daily, so that the number of disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem (Acts 6:6-7; Acts 2:47) [1][3]. That growth was measurable — about three thousand souls added in one day, and later about five thousand men (Acts 2:41; Acts 4:4) [3]. So a bishop must know his duty toward church growth and carry it out with all his heart as unto the Lord, since Jesus said, "I will build my church and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" [1].

Practically, the books say to create a Church Growth Office that monitors the things relevant to growth — attendance, income, number of branches, lay and full-time pastors, shepherds, small groups, active members, weekly converts [3]. Growth comes through a systematic campaign of aggressive activities with a specific purpose, not by osmosis [4]. And take your "tangerine segments" — the naturally formed groups like the choir, ushers, or neighbourhood people — and make those groups grow, for if your choir is very large, your church will be very large [6]. Don't be in a hurry; the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, the least of seeds that becomes a great tree (Matthew 13:31-32) [5][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 62 and 64 of *The Gift Of Governments*, chapters 4 and 26 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapter 7 of *The Mega Church* and chapter 20 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 13:31-32; Acts 2:41; Acts 2:47; Acts 4:4; Acts 6:6-7; Acts 13:44.

items.question: Why do some pastors keep moving from place to place or stay far from home?
items.book: Jezebel, A Woman Out Of Order
items.text:
Some pastors move because they are searching for the place God has designed for them, where they will become fruitful. Jacob recognized that the Lord was in a certain place, and Isaac moved from place to place until he found Rehoboth, saying, "now the Lord hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land" (Genesis 26:22) [1]. A bishop may also transfer pastors who are unable to breakthrough and flourish in a town, or who are unable to live in purity there, to break a cycle of barrenness or immorality [7].

Others move for painful reasons. Some move from place to place trying to control a difficult marriage, or live far away to stay away from their marital home, or abandon their church and move to another country while it looks like mission work — like Elijah, on the run [8]. And some deliberately move from church to church so that their history or background is not known [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 10 of *Opportunities*, chapter 59 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 18 of *The Beauty The Beast and The Pastor*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 26:22; Genesis 28:16; 1 Kings 21:18-19; Matthew 16:26; Titus 1:5.

items.question: How old were Jesus' disciples when he called them?
items.text:
The books give us some clues here. From the Mishnah's stages of a young man's life, most of the disciples may have been below eighteen, with some as young as fifteen, since Peter is the only one known to have been married [1][3]. Peter himself likely started his ministry at about the age of twenty, since Jesus paid the temple tax only for Himself and Peter, and the tax applied to those twenty and up (Exodus 30:12-14) [5]. The disciples were probably younger than Jesus, and Peter, James, John and the others became apostles when they were young men [2].

That said, the books also note there is no evidence in Scripture for a specific age for any of the disciples, and these are clues drawn from the gospels and Jewish culture rather than certainties [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 10 of *The Word Of My Patience* and chapter 6 of *Seven Great Principles*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 30:12-14; Matthew 8:14-15; Matthew 17:24-27; Luke 5:10; Luke 7:28; 1 Corinthians 4:1; Revelation 3:10.

items.question: How can I deal with people in my church who criticize the pastor behind his back?
items.text:
Our books speak to this plainly. Criticism of the pastor behind his back is not a small thing — it is listed among the reasons people withhold their tithes, and such people hold an unspoken standard of living they expect their pastor never to cross [2]. The books also say that a church full of critical and faultfinding people is one of the highest kinds of demonic infiltration in the church [7].

The remedy given is not prayer or fasting but removal: "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out; yea strife and reproach shall cease" (Proverbs 22:10), and the books describe casting out as dismissing, expelling, or laying off the scoffer [4]. At the same time, the books counsel patience where the criticism comes from immaturity — Jesus did not rebuke the disciples for abandoning Him, understanding it as a stage of development, and gave them another chance [5]. A senior pastor is told to check mild disloyalty before it grows into serious rebellion, sometimes by letting the person go through the "school of hard knocks" and carry head-ship himself [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich*, chapters 4 and 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant* and chapter 10 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 1:1; Proverbs 22:10; Proverbs 23:7; Proverbs 26:15; Mark 14:27-31; Romans 13:1.

items.question: What does the Bible say about people who were born and raised in the church?
items.text:
What a blessing it is to be born in the house of God. The eighty-seventh psalm speaks of the spiritual blessings that follow young people who were born in the house, and it says "This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her" (Psalm 87:5), so those born in the house are going to be greatly established [2]. Glorious things are spoken of you because you were born in the house, and you will have a lasting foundation; Satan may threaten to destroy you with sex, but you will stand sure because you have a solid foundation in holiness [1].

The Lord shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there (Psalm 87:6), so you will be counted among those who are great in the house of God, and when the lists of His great men are made, those born in the house with a good foundation of serving the Lord when young will be included [1]. Even the music is different: "As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee" (Psalm 87:7), so the children grow up loving Christian music and are never polluted by the music of the world [1]. Being born in a particular church and growing up in it to become a leader in the same church is a prophetic blessing God is giving you [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Ready@20*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 87:1-7.

items.question: How can I show appreciation to the people in my life before it's too late?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly to this. We need to value people and things before we lose them, and many are those who kneel at graves weeping, grieving not only because the person is dead but because they didn't show appreciation while they were alive [1][2]. So look into your life and see whether there is anybody you need to value, and if it is not too late, locate them and find a suitable way of expressing appreciation [1][2].

Honour before it is too late — Mary honoured Jesus in time, and if you want to honour someone, rush to do so now [3]. One pastor felt convicted to seek out a great man of God, find his hotel, and present him a special offering; two weeks later the man had died, and he realised God had urged him to honour him before it was too late [3].

And remember that the deepest thanks is not words alone: the only way you can say "Thank you" is with your life, giving something genuine and real, as Romans 12:1-2 says [5][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 4 of *Frugality*, chapter 13 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 4 of *How Can I Say Thanks*.

Scriptures referenced: Romans 12:1-2.

items.question: How do I experience God's presence when I don't feel Him near?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and I want to walk with you through what our books actually say.

The presence of God is real and can be felt — Jehovah Shammah means "The Lord is there," and it is possible to grow in your ability to experience Him, in your room, in your meetings, at home [2][4]. His presence is like dew: invisible, yet you can see its effects in the watering and growth of your life [2]. So even when you don't feel Him, His presence may be at work unseen.

Our books also point to things that draw His presence near. Where salvation and redemption are preached and believed, the presence of God is felt — you can practically invoke His presence by believing in the atoning blood of Jesus [5][8]. And being under a covering matters: a man of God with no covering will not experience the presence of God in his ministry, and it is important to be under a covering if you want to experience His presence [3]. The books also warn that sins of the flesh and sins of pride cause many to lose the presence of God [6].

If what you're really asking is why you don't feel Him in a particular season or situation, our books have not directly addressed that.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 13 of *The Anointing and the Presence* and chapters 11 and 14 of *Steps to God's Presence*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 33:14-15; Ezekiel 48:35; Hosea 14:5-6; Zechariah 11:12; Matthew 27:8-9; Luke 5:17; 1 Corinthians 1:27-29.

items.question: How can I keep from becoming bitter and turning away from God when I go through hard times?
items.text:
What you're asking about is real, and our books speak to it plainly. Suffering is a test that brings out what is in you [5], and one of the very first stops on the journey is the bitter waters of Marah — it is there that many fall away, so do not fall away because of the bitterness you experience in ministry [4]. Do not turn against God when you receive the contradiction of sinners; Jesus Himself endured the contradiction of sinners and showed us how to endure it, as Hebrews 12:3 says [1].

Practically, the books tell you not to become a murmurer or complainer, for murmuring reveals a bad attitude and keeps you from the call of God [6]. Instead, put away all bitterness and wrath and anger, and be kind and tender-hearted, forgiving each other just as God in Christ has forgiven you, as Ephesians 4 says [7]. When you walk in forgiveness you attract God's mercy, but when bitterness is in your spirit you no longer receive from God and He no longer answers your prayers [2]. So maintain a sweet spirit, and remember that if you survive this and go on, you will become one of the few that are chosen [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*, chapter 10 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapters 26 and 30 of *Why Few Are Chosen* and chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 8:2; Hebrews 12:3.

items.question: How can I pray more effectively?
items.text:
Prayer that works is not doodling and dawdling — it is effectual, fervent prayer, and James 5:16 says the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much [1]. So let your prayers be guided by the Word of God, praying the very prayers recorded in Scripture, like the powerful prayer in Ephesians 1:17-19 and the prayer in Ephesians 3:15-19 to be grounded in love [1]. Pray fervently — ardently, with passion and feeling, so that anyone watching could describe your prayer as burning and eager [3]. Spend hours praying in tongues, as Paul boasted, "I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all" (1 Corinthians 14:18) [3]. And let prayer be a two-way affair: speak to the Holy Spirit and hear His voice, for as Jesus said, the Comforter "shall teach you all things" (John 14:26) [3].

You can also pray without ceasing, on the bus, in the office, in the shower, keeping in touch with God all day [4]. For prayer to be effective it must be habitual, continuing in troubled times and in times of peace [4]. It is important to enter your closet and pray alone, and to develop the ability to pray four times a day — morning, afternoon, evening and all-the-time [6]. Jesus Himself rose a great while before day and went to a solitary place to pray (Mark 1:35) [6][8], and He continued all night in prayer to God (Luke 6:12,13) [6]. Watching and praying — staying awake at night to pray — is more important than fasting and praying, and those who watch and pray pray far more [8].

items.question: If I do good things for others, how will I be rewarded?
items.book: He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this in two ways, and I'll give you both.

First, do not look to people for your reward. A leader looks to God for rewards, for Scripture says, "Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man doeth, the same shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free" (Ephesians 6:8) [2]. Do not expect much from people; expect your rewards from God [2]. People are often ungrateful and forgetful, and even those you have blessed may repay you with evil, as Jeremiah found when they dug a pit for him [1][7]. So do not be surprised by ingratitude [2].

Second, there is a reward in the work itself. God has seen your faithfulness in things that were not your own, and He rewards that faithfulness with more work — being given your own to steward, as Luke 16:12 says, "And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?" [5]. And be warned, God will not reward you because you did many good things, but because you obeyed Him [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How Can I Say Thanks*, chapter 101 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 26 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 5 of *WOM15. The Reward for Hard Work is More Work* and chapter 5 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*.

Scriptures referenced: Jeremiah 18:19-20; Luke 14:26; Luke 16:12; John 10:32; Ephesians 6:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-2.

items.question: Why do the people closest to a pastor, like family and his wife, often have a hard time receiving from his ministry?
items.text:
This is a painful thing, and our books speak to it plainly. It is called familiarity: those who know you best can be the very ones who cannot receive from you. Jesus Himself could do no mighty work in His hometown, and they were offended at Him, saying, "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" (Mark 6:1-3, 5) [6]. Moses, who commanded the pillar of fire and cloud, could not impress his own sister Miriam [6].

The books name the groups who often suffer this. Relatives say, "Is this not Azoyzoy's son? We carried him when he was a baby" [8]. Pastors' wives often suffer severe familiarity, like Michal, who was not impressed with her husband when everyone else was [8]. Colleagues say, "Is this not Dag? We know him and we know his class" [6][8]. And some simply sit at the back, no longer intrigued or excited, observing from a distance [8]. Familiarity even carves out a road of ministry, directing the anointed away from colleagues, friends and family toward the outsiders, the poor and the forgotten [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *Church Planting* and chapter 13 of *Ministerial Barrenness*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 6:1-3; Mark 6:5.

items.question: I keep saying hurtful things when I am angry. How do I control my mouth?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. The tongue is "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:8), and no man can tame his tongue on his own — it takes the Holy Spirit to help the believer control it [3]. So this is not a battle you win by sheer willpower; you need Him.

Practically, the books say to give no place to the devil and no opportunity to your flesh (Ephesians 4:27), and to flee rather than stand and fight when you are tempted [6]. They also warn that anger and wrath are signs of lingering unforgiveness, and that these must be put away, being kind and tenderhearted and forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven you (Ephesians 4:31-32) [5]. And "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Ephesians 4:26) — don't let silence or offence sit and deepen the strain [1].

One caution from the books: when a bitter person speaks, it affects, influences and poisons others [5]. So the mouth is tied to the heart, and the heart needs the forgiving work of God.

items.question: How can I stay close to God and keep bearing fruit in my life?
items.text:
What a good thing to long for, pastor. The books speak to this very plainly: draw near to God and He will draw near to you (James 4:8), and the closer you get to God, the closer you are to bearing fruit [1]. Abiding in Christ is essential — "He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit" (John 15:5) — and the longer you stay in God, the more fruitful you become [1].

Closeness is a law of fruit bearing: as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself except it abide in the vine, so it is with you (John 15:4-5) [3]. Staying connected to Jesus is the master key; human effort can never substitute for being deeply connected to Him, and disconnection and detachment are the master keys to withering [2][4]. So watch your connection to the tree, for it is your close attachment that leads to life [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Fruitfulness (2022)*, chapter 6 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make* and chapter 14 of *Victory Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 127:1; Mark 12:34; John 15:4-6; James 4:8; Revelation 1:20.

items.question: How can I be sure I really know the Lord and won't be turned away from heaven?
items.text:
What a tender and important question, pastor. Our books speak to it plainly: the danger is real, because many serve the Lord without knowing Him in reality, and not knowing God is the basis for being thrown out of heaven [1]. Jesus Himself says, "I never knew you: depart from me" to people who prophesied, cast out devils, and did wonderful works in His name (Matthew 7:22-23) [2][3]. So it is possible to be a member and do great things but not know God [3][4].

The way the books point to is a personal relationship with Him, and they say a daily quiet time is what makes that relationship — nothing else can [3][4]. Coming to church a thousand times is different from a personal, one-to-one interaction with the Lord, and it is this personal interaction most Christians lack [3][4]. A daily quiet time will prevent you from going to hell and will save you from the delusion that working for God is the same as knowing Him [3][4]. It is up to us to draw near to Him daily, for as James 4:8 says, "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" [4]. And through the blood of Jesus you are cleansed from your sins and can get to know God [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Weeping and Gnashing*, chapter 30 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:21-23; Luke 13:25-28; 2 Timothy 1:8-9; James 4:8; Revelation 3:20.

items.question: What does the wind of the Holy Spirit do in a person's life?
items.text:
The wind of the Spirit does many things in a person's life. It blows away demonic powers that have invaded your church, as the locusts were taken away by a mighty strong west wind (Exodus 10:16-19) [2]. It can blow away death, as God made a wind to pass over the earth so the waters assuaged (Genesis 8:1-3) [1]. It makes a way for you when you seem trapped, as the Lord caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind (Exodus 14:21) [1][3]. It causes anything that displeases God to wither, like the seven ears blasted with the east wind (Genesis 41:22-23) [2]. It dries up the evil springs of the enemy, for the wind of the Lord shall come up from the wilderness and his spring shall become dry (Hosea 13:15) [3]. It destroys the enemy's forces, for the Lord will raise up a destroying wind against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:1-2) [5]. And it brings in the supplies you need, as through the wind of the Spirit Moses was able to feed two million people [5].

When the wind of the Holy Spirit blows on you, you start to see, you start to hear and you start to feel [7]. There will be activity, for a sign of the presence of the breath of the Spirit is lots of activity [7]. And there will be growth, for wherever there is life there is growth [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Flow in the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 7:21-22; Genesis 8:1-3; Genesis 41:22-23; Exodus 10:16-19; Exodus 14:21-22; Psalms 35:5; Psalms 104:29; Isaiah 11:15-16; Jeremiah 51:1-2; Hosea 13:15.

items.question: What can I learn from Esther about helping others even when I'm comfortable?
items.text:
Friend, the books hold up Esther as a picture of someone who was comfortable but was called to help "others." She had been favoured, chosen, and given access to every privilege, yet her uncle reminded her there were other people outside the palace, just like her, who were about to be slaughtered [2]. The warning was plain: if she held her peace, deliverance would arise from another place, but she and her father's house would be destroyed — and who knew whether she had come to the kingdom for such a time as this [5][8].

So the lesson is that your comfort and position have a reason. Perhaps God made you who you are so you can help "others" [1]. A virtuous woman stretches out her hand to the poor and reaches forth her hands to the needy (Proverbs 31:20) [3]. And it may cost you something: Esther was prepared to lay down her life, saying, "if I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:15-16) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *Others*, chapter 33 of *Daughter, You Can Make It* and chapter 14 of *The Art of Following*.

Scriptures referenced: Esther 4:13-16; Proverbs 31:20.

items.question: Why is it so hard to leave a church that feels like family?
items.text:
It's hard because a church that has become a family is exactly what Jesus described: those who do the will of the Father are His brother, sister, and mother (Matthew 12:48-50), and He made these people His family [1]. When leadership builds the church as a family, no one leaves a family until they die, and faithfulness unto death becomes a natural occurrence [1].

Every family has its problems, conflicts, and misunderstandings, but there is simply no way you can leave your family — you are part of it whether you like it or not, and a misunderstanding with your uncle does not lead you to change your name [2]. So members are taught that hurts should not make them change churches, because family members belong together in a lifetime commitment [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Be Thou Faithful Unto Death* and chapter 11 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:5; Matthew 12:48-50; 1 Corinthians 3:9; Ephesians 5:31.

items.question: Can God heal emotional wounds and mental problems that medicine can't fix?
items.book: Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books speak to this clearly. A daily dose of God's powerful Word will bring healing to every inner wound, and the Lord Himself says, "I am the Lord your doctor, the Lord your healer, the Lord your physician" — Jehovah Rophe [1][2]. As Psalm 147:3 says, "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds" [3][6]. The broken-hearted are those with emotional and psychological setbacks, and Jesus' healing ministry specifically mentioned healing them, as Luke 4:18 shows [4].

The books also say plainly that God is not against medicine — the wisdom for medical science is from Him, and the two streams of healing are ordained of God and not contrary to each other [5][8]. So medicine is not the enemy of your healing; but where medicine has no real cure, especially in the mind and emotions, God is able to heal what man cannot heal [2][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapters 1, 14, 15 and 17 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Kings 2:19-22; Psalms 23:3; Psalms 107:20; Psalms 147:3; Jeremiah 17:14; Mark 5:2-3; Luke 4:18; John 9:1-2; 1 Corinthians 1:24.

items.question: How can I spend time with God every morning without getting bored?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
What a good desire, pastor. The books speak directly to this. The morning time is meant to be a relationship, not a duty — during quiet time you develop the most important relationship of your life, and a natural relationship develops between any two people who spend quality time together [2]. When you draw near to God, He draws near to you, as James 4:8 says [2].

Boredom often creeps in when the time becomes only reading. So vary how you feed your spirit: let the Word enter through a daily Quiet Time, Bible study and Bible reading, and also by listening to preaching and watching services, since faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17) [1]. Praying in tongues also builds you up [1], and praying at dawn will help you read your Bible and grow in the Word, so that your knowledge of it greatly increases [4]. A daily dose of the Word will increase your faith [7], and a daily quiet time drives away weariness, dejection and depression — the Word is like rain and snow that cools and refreshes, as Isaiah 55:10 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell*, chapters 3 and 6 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day* and chapter 13 of *Everything By Prayer 

Nothing Without Prayer*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 3:1-3; Isaiah 55:10; Mark 1:34-36; Romans 1:16; Romans 10:17; James 4:8; 1 Peter 2:2.

items.question: How can I tell if someone is really a Christian or just going to church?
items.text:
You can tell by their fruits, as Matthew 7:20 says: "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them." We can distinguish genuine Christians from counterfeit Christians by looking at their fruits [1][2][3][4]. If, by their spiritual activity, others just like them are brought to the Lord and discipled, then this fruit shows that they are real; but if they have no converts to show for their Christianity, then there must be something missing [1][2][3].

Church membership does not prove someone is a genuine Christian at all, and if all their Christianity is going to church on Sundays, they are missing a great deal of spiritual activity [1][5]. Real Christianity takes place outside the church after Sundays, with each weekday having its share of prayer, worship, Bible reading and labouring for the Lord [1][5]. As 2 Corinthians 13:5 says, "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith" [1][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Many Are Called* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 7:20; 2 Corinthians 13:5.

items.question: Why can't I get to heaven by being a good person?
items.text:
Being a good person and doing good works is not the way to Heaven; good works will not take you to Heaven, because the only way is through the blood of Jesus [1][2][7]. As Isaiah 64:6 says, all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and as it is written, there is none righteous, no, not one [1][2][3]. We are saved by grace through faith, and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast (Ephesians 2:8-9) [3][7]. You cannot be good enough to qualify for Heaven; our best is not good enough [3].

That said, the same Scripture that says salvation is not by works also says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:8-10) [3][4]. So after we are saved, we get into the good works Christ has prepared for us [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 65 and 111 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 1 of *Tell Them* and chapters 2 and 3 of *Church Planting*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 11:16; Proverbs 11:4-5; Isaiah 42:17; Isaiah 64:6; Matthew 7:21-22; Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6-7; Luke 9:24; Acts 4:12; Romans 3:10 and 3 more.

items.question: What happens if I dishonour my husband?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this. Dishonour brings a loss of your place: Vashti did not honour her husband, she lost her position, and she was replaced by a more humble person — the reward for dishonour is to lose your place [1][3]. Dishonour also results in being lightly esteemed, for as 1 Samuel 2:30 says, "they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed" [1].

There is more. Dishonour opens a door to demonic invasion — Jesus said He had no devil because He honoured His Father (John 8:49-50), and when Vashti dishonoured her husband, the devils of demotion invaded her life [2]. It also brings obscurity, for Proverbs 20:20 says whoever curses his father or mother has his lamp put out in obscure darkness [6]. And a wife who does not adapt herself to her husband is dishonouring him [4]; when your husband is disgraced, you are disgraced as well, so wives must not blacken their husbands' reputation [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 6 and 11 of *Those Who Honour You* and chapter 31 of *Daughter, You Can Make It*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 32:17; Ruth 3:1-4; 1 Samuel 2:30; Esther 1:15-20; Proverbs 20:20; Luke 22:3; John 8:49-50.

items.question: Why does the Bible warn against trying to get rich?
items.book: Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich
items.text:
The books give several reasons. Ill-gotten riches can cut your life short — "he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days" (Jeremiah 17:10-11) [1]. Earthly riches can turn you into a fool, as in the parable of the man with full barns to whom God said, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luke 12:16-21) [1][2]. Riches are linked to many temptations and traps: "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:9-10) [3][4]. Riches can prevent you from taking up your cross and following Jesus — "how hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" (Mark 10:17-23) [5]. And riches are deceptive: "the deceitfulness of riches... choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful" (Mark 4:19) [5].

So the instruction stands: "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom" (Proverbs 23:4) [7]. Instead, labour to be blessed, for "the blessing of the Lord makes rich" (Proverbs 10:22), and within that blessing you will have more than enough and to spare [2][6][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 4 of *Labour to be blessed…labour not to be rich* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 23:4; Ecclesiastes 5:14-16; Jeremiah 17:10-11; Matthew 1:21; Mark 4:19; Mark 10:17-23; Luke 12:15-21; 1 Timothy 6:9-10.

items.question: How do I meditate on the Bible and get something out of it during my quiet time?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
Brother, meditation is simply thinking through and soberly reflecting on what you have read, and Paul told Timothy to think about the Word of God — "Consider what I say; and the Lord give thee understanding in all things" (2 Timothy 2:7) [1][2][3]. If you do not think about what you are reading, you will lose a major blessing of the Word of God [1][2][3].

Practically: read the passage slowly, don't read a very long passage unless it is necessary, and stop at any verse that strikes you and think about it — God's Word is so powerful that only a single word in a verse is enough to change your life, so each quiet time should be a search for that single word [1][2][3]. Think about the meanings of the words you are reading, and think about how the Scripture applies to life in your generation [1][2][3]. Whisper to the Holy Spirit, saying, "Help me Holy Spirit to understand your Word. Father, give me the Spirit of Wisdom and Revelation" (Ephesians 1:17) [1][2][3]. Then decide on a practical way to implement what you have learnt, for without thinking of a way to apply the Scripture directly you will often not benefit from your quiet time [1][2][6].

You may also stay there and turn it over in your mind till the full revelation comes to you, for through the Holy Spirit many verses will become revelations, counsel and supernatural guidance to you every day [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers*, chapter 3 of *The Secret* and chapter 10 of *One Thousand Micro Churches*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:18; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Timothy 2:7.

items.question: How can I cooperate with the anointing for dreams and visions?
items.text:
The key is to accept, believe in, and flow with the visions and dreams God gives you, rather than despising them [1]. Daniel wrote his dream down because he respected it, and writing something down shows how seriously you take it [1]. So don't dismiss a dream just because it seems vague or strange — the drive to obey these visions is the drive toward the anointing [2].

Obeying what God shows you is central: most of us have dreams and visions we do not obey, and if we obeyed them we would experience the anointing [2]. Cornelius obeyed his vision and Peter obeyed his, and one thing led to another until Cornelius and his household received the anointing [2][3]. Flow with your dreams and visions, because they are God's instruments encouraging you along the road to the anointing [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 15 of *The Art of Following* and chapter 6 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Daniel 7:1-4; Acts 10:7-8; Acts 10:13-15; Acts 10:32; Acts 10:48.

items.question: How do I get angels to intervene in my situation when I pray?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this plainly: prayer itself is the great and definite way of securing angelic intervention. Jesus said He could pray to the Father and be given more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:52-54), and where there is prayer there is angel activity — prayer activates and releases angels [1][2]. Angels are drawn to prayer; they will come to the very room you are praying in, whether you are on a mountain or in a valley [3][6].

The books also give examples: an angel came to Zachariah because his prayer was heard (Luke 1:8-16) [2][8]; angels ministered to Jesus in the wilderness and in Gethsemane as He prayed (Luke 22:40-44) [3][6]; Peter was delivered from prison while many were gathered together praying (Acts 12:1-12) [4]; and Cornelius was told his prayers had come up as a memorial before God (Acts 10) [4]. There is also another well-known way the books mention — hospitality and entertainment, for some have entertained angels unawares (Genesis 19:1-3) [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *Prayer Changes Things*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 19:1-3; Daniel 10:1-15; Matthew 26:52-54; Luke 1:8-16; Luke 22:40-44; Acts 12:1-12; Revelation 15:1.

items.question: How should I respond when people constantly accuse and criticize me for serving God?
items.book: One of You is a Devil
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly, and the first thing they say is that you are not alone in it. Everyone who takes up the call of God is truly an honourable person, and yet ministers are vilified and denigrated constantly; Moses and our Lord Jesus both sustained relentless attacks in the form of complaints and accusations [6]. Jesus was perfect and yet He was accused until His life was snuffed out [6].

The books urge you to deal with the accuser rather than let him flourish nearby, because when accusations are silenced, salvation, strength, the kingdom of our God, and the power of Christ are released (Revelation 12:10) [1]. Accusations are also called "the pointing of the finger," and your light will break forth like the dawn and there will be recovery if you put away the pointing of the finger (Isaiah 58:8-9) [2]. David shows a decisive response: when Michal re-described his worship as shameful, he refused to accept that kind of talk in his house and said he would play before the LORD (2 Samuel 6:20-21) [8].

At the same time, be careful how you receive an accusation, for Scripture says not to receive an accusation against an elder except before two or three witnesses (1 Timothy 5:19) [7]. And guard your own heart from fault-finding, for the servant with one talent did nothing because he found fault with his master, calling him a hard man (Matthew 25:24); those who criticize God's servants do so at their own risk [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1, 5 and 8 of *Those Who Accuse You*, chapter 5 of *Weeping and Gnashing* and chapter 4 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 2 Samuel 6:20; Isaiah 58:8-9; Daniel 10:13; Matthew 25:24; 1 Timothy 5:19; Revelation 12:10.

items.question: Can a pastor lead a group of people he pulled away from their church into a new one?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. The question every rebel leader must be asked is, "Can you lead these people?" and the answer given is no — the people you lead will never be loyal to you, because they have learned how to rebel and overthrow legitimate authority and will practise it when they get the chance [1]. You will not be able to silence their rebellious way of speaking, quench their murmurings, or prevent the hatred and conspiracies around you, because you have sown the seeds of instability and rebellion and taught your followers how to dislodge legitimate leaders [1].

The books also show this working out in practice: a pastor who broke away and started his own church near the one he had led saw others follow his example, and a "domino spirit of rebellion" was released into the team of pastors [2]. In another case, a pastor who left an associate with the old congregation later had that associate steal the hearts of the people and lead them to break away from him [4]. And where a breakaway leader appointed eleven new pastors, this was described as doing what Jeroboam did, ordaining men of the lowest sort, which makes nonsense of spiritual authority and confuses the flock (1 Kings 12:28-31) [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 5, 6 and 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Kings 12:28-31.

items.question: Why are Jesus' words so much greater than the words of other great teachers?
items.book: The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make
items.text:
The books say His words are greater because of who He is: they are the words of the Son of God, and no other man ever spoke like He did [3][4]. Where other teachers give us truths mixed with what is trivial or absurd, He eliminated the trivial, the temporal, and the false, selecting only the eternal and universal [8]. As Bernard Ramm put it, no other man's words have the appeal of Jesus' words because no other man can answer those fundamental human questions as Jesus answered them — who is God, does He love me, how can I be forgiven, where will I go when I die [1][7].

His words are also anointed, so that they changed the lives of those who heard them, and they are full of love and kindness [5]. They have passed into law, doctrines, proverbs, and consolations, but they have never passed away, and no human teacher ever dared to claim eternity for his words [1][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Words of Jesus* and chapter 5 of *The Top Ten Mistakes that Pastors Make*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 12:36; Matthew 18:21-22; Luke 4:36; John 6:63; John 7:46.

items.question: How do I know if God has hidden a gift in me that others can't see yet?
items.book: Lord I Know You Need Somebody
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this very thing. Your gift being hidden is not a sign it isn't there — God is the One who conceals the potential He has placed in you, and every great man of God is like a hidden treasure yet to be revealed [1]. Your ministry is like a mustard seed, the least of all seeds, which grows into the greatest among herbs (Matthew 13:31-32), and like leaven hidden in a meal that will eventually influence the whole dough [1].

You can also look at how you respond to the Word. The hearing ear and the seeing eye are both made by the Lord (Proverbs 20:12), and if preaching and teaching are a joyful sound to you, that is evidence of the gift of seeing and hearing [6]. And if you already perceive that God has given you some gift, that itself makes you a candidate for more, for "whosoever hath, to him shall be given" (Matthew 13:12) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Lord I Know You Need Somebody*, chapter 2 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 12 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 20:12; Matthew 13:11-12; Matthew 13:16; Matthew 13:31-32; Matthew 13:44.
