items.question: Why does God allow trials and suffering in the lives of believers?
items.text:
God allows trials and suffering in the lives of believers for many reasons, and our books speak to this plainly.

Suffering is part of our calling, not a sign that God is angry with you. As Philippians 1:29 says, it is given to us not only to believe on Christ but also to suffer for His sake, and 1 Thessalonians 3:3 says we are appointed to it [5]. Paul said he was appointed a preacher and apostle, and for that cause he also suffered [1]. Suffering also proves you are a good Christian, since 1 Timothy 4:10 says we labour and suffer reproach because we trust in the living God, and 2 Timothy 3:12 says all who live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution [2].

It follows the example of Jesus, who suffered for us and left us an example that we should follow His steps (1 Peter 2:21) [3]. It breaks the power of sin, for 1 Peter 4:1 says he that has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin [3]. It pleases God, as Isaiah 53:10 says it pleased the Lord to bruise him [4]. It tests and humbles us, as Deuteronomy 8:2 says God led Israel in the wilderness to humble them and test them, to know what was in their heart [8]. And it is a gift that makes us humble, so that we can count it all joy when we enter various testings (James 1:2) [8].

One caution our books give: a minister should suffer only according to the will of God (1 Peter 4:19), and it is important to seek His will about why you are suffering, since you may be in His will or you may be suffering the fruits of your own disobedience [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Deuteronomy 8:2; Isaiah 53:10; Acts 9:15-16; 2 Corinthians 1:9; 2 Corinthians 12:7; Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 1:29; 1 Thessalonians 3:3; 1 Timothy 4:10 and 6 more.

items.question: And how should I deal with them once I notice it?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't just happen overnight — becoming disloyal is a process, and most people are unaware of it, so you must learn to detect it both in yourself and in those you work with [2]. The Lord showed eight stages: the independent spirit, offence, passivity, being critical, being political, deception, open rebellion, and destruction [4]. The first stage is subtle — the person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important [2]. There are also outward symptoms, since loyalty and disloyalty are things of the heart and are best detected by watching for signs [6]: disobedience, which is an outward manifestation of a disloyal heart [6], scorning [6], and inflexibility — the stubborn person who won't go beyond what is stipulated, won't adapt, and won't take correction when confronted, as Saul argued with Samuel instead of receiving the word [3]. A leader is also often subjected to hypocritical advice and lying praises, which is why a good leader must learn the signs of disloyalty [1].

As for dealing with it, the books give more than one method. One is expulsion: the biblical treatment for scornful people is expulsion, and failure to dismiss people is like failing to do a surgery that will save your life — when the author used this method, a new spirit of loyalty entered the church [5]. Another is the marking and avoiding method, from Romans 16:17-18, which teaches that people who cause divisions must be noted and avoided at all costs; to mark means to brand or label so the person stands out and can be recognized from afar [5]. The books also say a disloyal person is unfit for the work of God and worthless for good work of any kind, so you rather have to protect yourself from disloyal people [7]. And a bad assistant who is happy that things have gone wrong must be displaced and replaced [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*, chapters 7 and 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 6 of *Those who are mad* and chapter 8 of *Pillars of Loyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22-23; John 7:5; Romans 16:17-18; 1 Corinthians 4:2.

items.question: How can I know what my calling from God is?
items.book: What It Means to Become a Shepherd
items.text:
What a good thing to be asking, pastor. Our books say you come to know your calling by watching and observing what the Lord does with you and your life — you "see" your calling, as 1 Corinthians 1:26 puts it, and you discover it by noticing what works and where the anointing and fruit are [1]. It may not come as a voice thundering from Heaven; you watch your calling and flow with what God is doing [1].

Alongside that, you must be filled with the knowledge of His will concerning your calling, since your calling must be according to the will of God and not merely what you like doing [3]. And remember that you are called according to His purpose, so it is important not only to obey the call but to find out the purpose for which God called you [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)*, chapter 1 of *Predestination* and chapter 5 of *The Art of Hearing*.

Scriptures referenced: Matthew 10:6; 1 Corinthians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 1:26; 2 Corinthians 1:1; Colossians 1:9; 2 Timothy 1:9.

items.question: How can I be a good shepherd to the people in my church?
items.text:
What a good thing to want, pastor. Our books say plainly: if you are going to be a pastor, be a good one, doing it with all your might, as Ecclesiastes 9:10 says [2].

A good shepherd leads his sheep by going before them — anything you want your sheep to do, you must do it yourself first, as John 10:4 says, "he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him" [1][2]. That means being practically available for them to see and learn from you in every area of life and ministry [2]. A good shepherd also makes the sheep follow him and has them recognize his voice, for "my sheep hear my voice... and they follow me" (John 10:27) [1]. He knows his sheep and keeps them, so that none slip out of his hands, as Jesus said, "those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost" (John 17:12) [3]. And he is known by his sheep, opening up his life so they see how real he is [3].

The books also say a good shepherd is a winner of souls: he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the lost sheep, as Luke 15:4-7 describes [4], providing salvation and being a door for the sheep, for "by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved" (John 10:9) [5][8]. He gives life to the sheep, that they might have it more abundantly (John 10:10) [5], and he lays down his life for the sheep, as John 10:11 says [5][6]. He notices when the sheep are in trouble and prays for their deliverance from witchcraft, demons and diseases, anointing them with oil [6]. He also keeps the church family together and makes a way for his sheep to enter marriage, prosperity, and the ministry [3][8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 27 of *The Art of Shepherding*, chapter 13 of *What It Means to Become a Shepherd*, chapter 8 of *Church Growth* and chapter 2 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 9:10; Luke 15:4-32; John 10:3-4; John 10:7; John 10:9-12; John 10:27; John 17:12.

items.question: How can I serve closely in ministry without missing the spiritual blessings?
items.text:
Draw near and stay near, pastor. Being close is both an art and an act of humility, and pride or guilt can keep you standing at a distance when you are loved, wanted, and needed [8]. The Lord took the twelve "that they should BE WITH HIM" (Mark 3:14), so personal service has a "be with me" phase before any sending out [2].

But be careful of the danger in that closeness. Martha was near Jesus yet troubled about many things, while Mary chose the good part, the spiritual treasure that would not be taken away (Luke 10:41-42) [1][2]. So make sure you get the good part, and beware of familiarity, for even Jesus' own brethren did not believe in Him (John 7:5) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 16 of *Laikos Lay People and the Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 3:14; Luke 10:41-42; John 7:5; John 13:20; James 4:8.

items.question: How can I protect my church from wolves?
items.text:
The books give several ways. Be a pastor on fire: fire, passion and zeal are killers of wolves, and the power of deception cannot stand against the Holy Ghost and fire [1]. Fight aggressively, showing wolves that you are too dangerous to attack, and teach against every kind of disloyalty until the wolves are exposed [5]. Expect wolves and prepare for them, teaching loyalty and faithfulness, since churches that do not will struggle to survive a wolf attack [4]. Identify those who sympathise with a "departee" and send them away, as Abraham sent Ishmael away from Isaac (Genesis 25:5-6) [7]. And when you cannot physically protect the sheep, you may place a spiritual perimeter curse as a barrier, as Paul did against those preaching another gospel (Galatians 1:8-9) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 4 of *Those Who are Wolves* and chapter 10 of *Those who leave you*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 25:5-6; Psalms 31:18; Luke 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:12; 1 Peter 5:8.

items.question: Why do I need to hear from God for myself instead of just listening to my pastor?
items.text:
You need to hear from God for yourself because hearing Him directly is how you come to know Him — the more you hear from God, the more you know Him, and people are rejected because Jesus never knew them (Matthew 7:22-23) [1]. You may be in a good church with a good pastor leading the flock, but you will still need to hear the voice of God for yourself; if you do not hear from God directly you will get disconnected [1]. The children of Israel were brought to Mount Sinai to hear God's voice for themselves, and they failed that test [1].

That said, the books also speak of listening to your leader's messages. One passage teaches that pastors should listen to the messages their leader has preached, to learn how to preach, following those who through faith and patience inherit the promises (Hebrews 6:12), and to use them as resource material [2]. Another says to allow the Holy Spirit to lead you to what you must listen to, and to listen to people you genuinely believe are great [8]. So hearing God for yourself and learning from your leader's preaching are both set before you.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 4 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 33 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Exodus 20:19-21; Psalms 23:1; Matthew 7:22-23; Hebrews 6:12.

items.question: How do I deal with betrayal in the church?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this — betrayal in ministry is a real wound, and the books speak to it plainly.

First, know that betrayal is not a sign you've failed; it is part of ministry and part of life. Jesus was betrayed, and Paul was betrayed, so you should not expect to escape it [3][4]. If Judas is anything to go by, one out of twelve may be disloyal [4]. The painful part is that it comes from those supposedly close to you — "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me," as Psalm 41:9 says [3].

As for dealing with it, the books say you must be fierce and resolute, not benevolent toward the enemy, because disloyalty has the power to end a church and a ministry [7]. A person who betrays you is called a devil (John 6:70-71), and the way God dealt with the devil is the pattern: bind him, shut him up, and set a seal on him (Revelation 20:1-3) [6]. One method given is the teaching method — teaching the Word constantly as preventive management, since teaching fights deception, and it is the deceived who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [5]. Loyal lay people who do not earn money from the church are also a great support and will report what is going on in the congregation [3].

Do not be surprised, and do not expect gratitude from man; expect your rewards from God [3]. Get ready for envy, jealousy and betrayal as you rise, and to survive it you need determination and a great deal of faith [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *Church Growth*, chapter 54 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*, chapter 12 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*, chapter 33 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 12 of *The Church Must Send or It Will End*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 18:7-9; 2 Chronicles 32:25; Psalms 41:9; John 6:70-71; Revelation 20:1-3.

items.question: What does the Bible say about enjoying the money and blessings God gives you?
items.book: Why Non Tithing Christians Become Poor And Tithing Christians Become Rich
items.text:
Yes, the books speak to this. Ecclesiastes 6:1-2 describes it as an evil when a man is given riches and wealth but God does not give him power to eat thereof, so that a stranger eats it instead [4]. So spend money on yourself and use some of the wealth you have earned on yourself; that is part of enjoying your working life, and failure to eat your portion will make you hate life and hate work [4].

There is also joy in the Lord's blessing: the blessing of the Lord makes rich and adds no sorrow with it (Proverbs 10:22), unlike wealth that comes with sorrow [1]. And God takes pleasure in the prosperity of His servant, enjoying giving you money because you are His servant [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *He That Hath, To Him Shall Be Given: And He That Hath Not, From Him Shall Be Taken Even That Which He Hath*, chapter 9 of *Rules of Church Work (2nd Edition)* and chapter 6 of *It Is A Great Thing To Serve The Lord*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 36:11-12; Proverbs 10:22; Ecclesiastes 6:1-2; Ecclesiastes 9:9; Matthew 4:8.

items.question: How important is it to actually obey what Jesus says?
items.text:
It matters more than we often realize, pastor. All through the Bible, believing is equated with obeying — to believe in the gospel is to pledge yourself to obey the commandments of God, and obeying the gospel is all that God expects from us [4]. Jesus Himself said that the one who has His commandments and keeps them is the one who loves Him, and that He will manifest Himself to those who obey (John 14:21-25) [2].

Obedience is also the sign of your love and it provokes the anointing; there will be no manifestation towards those who do not obey [2]. And since we tend to weigh and assess every instruction, often wrongly, it is important to just obey every single commandment [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Not A Novice*, chapter 8 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 2 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 10:12-13; Matthew 22:36-40; John 14:21-25; 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9; 1 Peter 4:17.

items.question: How can I recognize when someone has gone from just being disloyal into open rebellion against God's servants?
items.text:
The books describe open rebellion as the last stage in the pattern of disloyalty, where a person openly attacks an authority figure he should rather honour [3]. It shows up as bizarre and inappropriate behaviour: attacking someone they previously hailed and honoured, insulting and accusing someone they once loved, dishonouring dignitaries, and spreading preposterous lies meant to demean and degrade God's servants [1]. Moses warned that this was coming, saying, "I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck" (Deuteronomy 31:27) [3].

It helps to remember that disloyalty is a process, not an overnight event, and most people don't even notice it happening in themselves or in those they work with [4]. The earlier stage is an independent spirit, where a person is still part of the church but does what he wants in spite of contrary instructions [4]. So watch for the movement from quiet independence toward open attack.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *Those who are mad* and chapter 2 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Deuteronomy 31:27-30.

items.question: What is the difference between the true church and the false church?
items.text:
The true church, the bride of Christ, is always inviting people to God and saying, "Come to Jesus" [1]. The false church says something completely different: "Stay here! Settle down! Celebrate! Prosper today! Secure yourself! Enrich yourself! Make yourself happy!" [1]. The true bride is evangelizing the world, while the false bride says, "Relax, take it easy, have fun, things are getting better for believers!" [1].

The passages also warn that many large and popular ministries preach doctrines that sound like the Gospel but are not, and that large-scale deception comes to God's people through false prophets [2]. One mark that separates true ministry from false is the fear of God rather than people, as Saul confessed, "I feared the people and listened to their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24) [3]. And Jesus said, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness" (John 8:12) — so we must be afraid of following a false light, for if you follow the wrong light you will pay dearly with your life [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 14 of *Make Yourselves Saviours of Men*, chapters 18 and 31 of *The Art of Shepherding* and chapter 73 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:24; Jeremiah 29:31; John 5:41; John 8:12.

items.question: Why is it so important for Christians to be part of a church assembly?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this plainly. The assembly is where your needs are met — material, emotional, marital, and family needs — for as Acts 4:33-34 shows, there was none among them that lacked [1][3]. It is also where you are protected: wild animals survive by staying together, and it is the isolated buffalo that the lions bring down, so in the assembly you are kept from being isolated [2].

The assembly is where you are edified and built up in knowledge, understanding, and faith, as 1 Corinthians 14:2-4 says [6], and where revelation and knowledge are imparted, as 1 Corinthians 14:6 says [1]. It is where healing power is present, for Luke 5:17 shows the power of the Lord was present to heal when they were assembled [2]. And it keeps you from turning into a mocker, since Jude 1:18-19 says mockers are those who separate themselves [3].

The books also warn that a coal separated from the fire dies out, and that it is dangerous not to fellowship regularly, as Hebrews 10:25 says [4]. So decide never to violate this basic principle of assembling, no matter what is happening in your life [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 6 of *One Thousand Micro Churches* and chapter 10 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 84:7; Proverbs 27:17; Luke 4:16; Luke 5:17; Acts 4:33-34; 1 Corinthians 14:2-4; 1 Corinthians 14:6; 1 Corinthians 14:26; Hebrews 10:25; Jude 18-19.

items.question: Why should I be a soul winner?
items.text:
Friend, the books give many reasons, and they all come back to this: it is the great commission, the great command given to us by our Lord Jesus Christ, who said, "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 28:18-20) [2]. It is the very heartbeat of Jesus, for "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10) [3][7].

You should be a soul winner because people are wasting their lives away without Jesus [1], and because we need to be reconciled to God — the whole world needs to be reunited with Him [1][4]. Soul winning also brings great joy and energizes Christians; the seventy returned again with joy (Luke 10:1-3,17) [5], and there is joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth [3]. It even prevents church splits, for when members are engaged in fruitful activities they have no time for petty quarrels [3]. And one day we will rejoice over the seeds we have sown, for "he that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him" (Psalms 126:6) [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Tell Them*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 126:6; Proverbs 14:12; Matthew 20:16; Matthew 22:14; Matthew 26:27-28; Matthew 28:18-20; Luke 10:1-3; Luke 10:17; Luke 15:14; Luke 19:10 and 13 more.

items.question: Why does God allow my enemies to stay instead of removing them?
items.book: WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous
items.text:
The books give more than one answer to that, and I'll lay them out as they stand.

One reason is testing and training: God allowed undefeated enemies to remain around Israel so they would have someone to spar with, so the generations who had not known war might be taught war, and so it could be found out whether they would obey the Lord's commandments [1]. The test of war is when God allows undefeated enemies to flourish around you [1].

Another reason is judgment: God made the enemies of Israel determined to fight, so they would be condemned to total destruction and killed without mercy, as He had commanded Moses (Joshua 11:20) [5]. God needs a reason to destroy your enemies, and so He has caused them to harden their hearts; the fight is not over because God wants them destroyed in the battle [5].

A third reason is promotion and good: God uses your enemies, and some of the greatest promotions come through them [6]. He uses them as an audience to see your greatness and victories (Psalm 23:5), and He uses their afflictions to work out good things in you — "It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes" (Psalm 119:71) [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapters 7 and 15 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Joshua 11:20; Judges 2:21-3:4; Psalms 23:5; Psalms 119:71; John 12:24.

He uses them as an audience to see your greatness and victories (Psalm 23:5), and He uses their afflictions to work out good things in you — "It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes" (Psalm 119:71).

items.question: How can someone turn to God in a moment of complete desperation?
items.text:
When things go from bad to worse, that is supposed to turn you towards God — your problems are meant to bring you towards Him [2]. Jonah, in his desperation, cried out to the Lord from the belly of the fish and said, "yet I will look again toward thy holy temple" (Jonah 2:1-4) [2]. The turning itself is repentance: humbling yourself, changing your mind, and going in the opposite direction, as the prodigal son did when he said, "I will arise and go to my father" (Luke 15:18) [2]. God commands all men everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30) [8].

Take heart too that God is near to the brokenhearted — "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit" (Psalm 34:18), and He is the God who comforts the depressed (2 Corinthians 7:6) [1]. He does not condemn you for speaking out your feelings in your desperation; Jesus Himself was overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death and prayed alone to His Father [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 22 of *Those who are mad* and chapters 5 and 43 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

items.question: How can I tell if someone in my church is a false friend or a pretender?
items.text:
Friend, this is a heavy question, and our books speak to it plainly. They tell us to watch for signs and symptoms, the way a doctor reads the body: notice people who are too quiet, for quiet people store up their thoughts and are dangerous [2][3][5]. Watch for those who seem to have two temperaments depending on who they are with, and for those who are too perfect and dignified in their presentation, since that is often a façade for hidden things [2]. A Judas is a liar who pretends to be telling the truth, a destroyer who pretends to be building, and one who cannot be trusted but pretends to be the most trustworthy person around [3].

The books also say to judge by actions and not by presentation, and to prove all things and hold fast to that which is good, as 1 Thessalonians 5:20 teaches [2][3][5]. People who say nothing in your presence but talk a lot when away from you are good examples of pretenders [3][5]. And be careful of one who seems to have completely ignored an offence and is even more gracious than before, for a pretender can feign forgiveness [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 2 of *Those Who Pretend, Intimidate And Are Familiar* and chapter 8 of *JUDAS
Who is he??*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 27:21-24; Joshua 9:3-16; Matthew 23:27-28; 1 Thessalonians 5:20.

items.question: What does the fear of man do to a person spiritually?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. Fear is not merely a mood or an attitude — it is an evil spirit, and its presence is a sign of demonic activity in your life [3][5]. When Adam rebelled, fear entered the human race for the first time, and rebels are full of fear and insecurity [1]. Fear takes away the soundness of your mind, so that you behave abnormally and cannot love as you should [2][3]. As 1 John 4:18 says, perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment, and the one who fears is not made perfect in love [7].

Fear also opens the door to many other evils — accusation, fault-finding, laziness, wickedness and poor performance — and fearful people become suspicious, accusative, insecure, and unable to take correction well [4]. It destroys love and fills a person with suspicion and uncertainty [7]. The good news is that God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of love, power and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7), and David prayed and the Lord delivered him from all his fears (Psalm 34:4) [3][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Rebel*, chapter 4 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 26 of *Now We Are At War* and chapter 9 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 3:9-10; Judges 7:3-4; Job 3:25; Psalms 34:4; 2 Timothy 1:7; 1 John 4:18.

items.question: Can I still serve God while I'm busy with my studies or other responsibilities?
items.book: How you can become a strong Christian
items.text:
Yes, you can. The books say plainly that being a student is just another "care" of this world which must not be allowed to choke God's Word and work, and that as a medical student the author successfully combined his schoolwork with his pastoral work, being a student and a pastor for years [3][5]. He never put the work of God aside because of school, and he asks, "Is being a medical student a curse? Does it mean that I cannot serve God anymore?" The answer is No [3][5].

Your love for God will guide you even while you study — it told the author to start a fellowship and go preaching in the halls of residence, and people may suggest you wait till you finish your studies, but love for God would not let him slow down [1][2]. The cares of life — paying bills, family responsibilities, exams — are legitimate, but God warns against becoming so overburdened that they dominate your life and kill your fruitfulness [3][4]. If you are too busy to be involved in winning souls, then you are simply too busy [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 6 of *How You Can Make Full proof of Your Ministry*, chapter 9 of *How you can become a strong Christian* and chapter 3 of *Bearing Fruit After Your Kind*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 16:15-17; Proverbs 22:13; Proverbs 30:18-19; Mark 4:19.

items.question: How do I become a better leader of people?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak to this directly. A good leader works on the people he leads until they become better human beings — leadership is not fancy titles but laboring on lives, as Jesus did with His disciples, so that people took knowledge of Peter and John that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13) [1]. A leader also reproduces himself in others, preparing them for the day he is no longer essential, as Jesus did when He told His disciples these things "when the time shall come" (John 16:4,5) [3].

Wisdom is the master key to the leadership skills you need, for by wisdom kings reign (Proverbs 8:15-16) [5]. And practically, value people, for people are the most valuable thing a leader has, and every person who feels undervalued will move away [7]. Learn to listen, let conversation center on others rather than yourself, be an encourager, say thank you, smile, and do not be partial, for the wisdom from above is without partiality (James 3:17) [6]. Bring peace between people and be at peace with others yourself, following peace with all men (Hebrews 12:14) [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 20, 23, 86, 121 and 126 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 4 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 1:8; 2 Samuel 18:3; Proverbs 8:15-16; Proverbs 8:20; Matthew 10:17; John 16:4-5; John 16:16; John 16:23; Acts 4:13 and 4 more.

items.question: How can a pastor grow an empty church?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. A pastor without anagkazo will have an empty church, and without it many churches will die a natural death; you must go out and compel people to come in, rather than sitting in church and inviting them [1]. The people who will fill empty churches are often not where invitation cards reach, so a strategy of going to the gutters, highways and bushes must be employed [1].

But growth also begins inside you: in the absence of a burning vision for a large church you will never have real church growth, and that burning vision is the invisible engine that drives a minister from a small church to a mega church [6][8]. You must also fight for it, for the gates of hell are postured against the church, and church growth is one of the most difficult things to do [2]. And spend your time with the twenty percent who bring the increase, for eighty percent of church growth comes from twenty percent of your members [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 27 of *Church Growth*, chapter 11 of *Attempt Great Things for God* and chapter 13 of *The Mega Church*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 29:18; Jeremiah 30:19; Acts 16:5.

items.question: How can I learn to work with different kinds of people to accomplish what God has called me to do?
items.book: What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent
items.text:
Friend, this is a good thing to ask, and our books speak to it plainly.

The heart of it is that the number of different groups you can work with reveals the magnitude of your calling — Nehemiah worked with forty-one different kinds of people, and Jesus came to die for all kindred, nations, tribes and tongues [1]. So aspire to that grace, and assess yourself by how many different groups you can work with [1]. Practically, that means developing the art of working with church members you preach to, with unbelievers whose expertise you need, with people older than you, and with lay people you do not pay [2]. It also means learning to work with women, with people who do not like each other but must work together, and with technical people [4]. Peter had to learn this too, for God showed him he should not call any man common or unclean (Acts 10:28), and Paul became all things to all men that he might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22,23) [5].

Two further things our books add. First, your limitations are overcome by recognizing the contribution of others — every joint supplies something, as Ephesians 4:16 says [7]. Second, becoming "another of the same kind" gives you access to methods and formulae that have worked for your kind, and that is how you find your way in the ministry [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapter 22 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*, chapter 14 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*, chapter 100 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 6 of *Many Are Called*.

Scriptures referenced: Acts 10:28; 1 Corinthians 9:22-23; Ephesians 4:16; Philippians 4:2.

items.question: Can my friends keep me from staying close to God?
items.text:
Yes, friends can affect your closeness to God, though the books put the responsibility on you. They warn that "they that are far from thee shall perish," and that closeness is a test of your survival, so you must fight to be close to God and to those who matter [3]. The books also say it is up to you to draw near to Him daily, since "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (James 4:8) [7].

At the same time, the books speak of closeness as something you learn from others: "Learn from close people! Watch what they do to come close!" [3]. And they note that being physically near someone does not make you spiritually near, since someone six thousand miles away may be closer than you sitting at his feet [1]. So the deciding factor is not merely who is around you, but whether you yourself keep drawing near to God.

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 16 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 6 of *WOM14. The Tests of the Righteous* and chapter 5 of *The Secret*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 65:4; Psalms 73:27-28; Mark 12:34; James 4:8.

items.question: Why do people who speak against God seem to prosper?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. One reason is that such prospering is itself determined: Daniel 11:35-36 says the king "shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done," and these people flourish because it is determined that they should [1]. Even the threats against Jesus were gathered "to do whatever your hand and your purpose predestined to occur" [1].

Another answer is that God often allows people to stray into His imperfect will and then receive a fitting judgment later: "abundance and apparent success does not mean that God is pleased with you," and money has never been a sign of His pleasure, since the devil also gives money to those who serve him [4]. Many sins are allowed to continue for years until the cup is full, and then judgment comes [8]. Yet the books also show swift judgment, as with Miriam, who was struck with leprosy almost immediately for her criticism [2]. And blasphemy against God was allowed for forty-two months, but at the end of that time it was no longer allowed [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 1 of *Predestination*, chapter 7 of *BEMA Judgment And Justice*, chapter 1 of *The Art of Hearing*, chapter 8 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 26 of *Why Few Are Chosen*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 12:1-15; Daniel 11:35-36; Romans 13:1; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How do I deal with disloyal people?
items.text:
The books speak plainly to this, and the heart of it is that you must not handle disloyalty in a spirit of benevolence, because all forms of disloyalty will end a church and a ministry [4]. The first and most important method is the teaching method: teach the Word of God regularly as a preventive measure, because teaching fights against deception, and it is only deceived people who go the way of Absalom or Lucifer [3].

When it comes to the disloyal person himself, the counsel is to wipe out disloyal people and all those associated with them, just as God cast out Lucifer and the angels associated with him (Revelation 12:9) [1]. Scorners are to be cast out, for Proverbs 22:10 says, "Cast out the scorner, and contention shall go out" [5]. Disloyal people are unfit for the work of God and worthless for good work of any kind, so you must protect yourself from them [6]. You must bind a "Judas" — that is, restrict him — rather than let him operate freely [7]. And it is essential to dismiss disloyal, disobedient or offending workers completely, even longstanding ones, while making financial provision so they can live and work elsewhere, so that the root of bitterness does not spread (Hebrews 12:15) [8].

items.question: How can I escape the curse on this earth and start living in God's blessings instead?
items.text:
What a good question to bring, pastor. The books speak to this directly, and they keep pointing to the same door.

The master key to overcoming the curse on this earth is God's wisdom from above, and anything in the Word of God is that wisdom — following any aspect of it will lift you above the curse [1][3]. Practically, that means seeking first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, as Matthew 6:33 says, and giving yourself to be led by the Holy Spirit, for as Romans 8:14 says, as many as are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God [3]. The anointing — the Holy Spirit — is the master key to breaking away from the curse, the burden and the yoke, and the yoke is destroyed because of the anointing, as Isaiah 10:27 says [4][6]. Israel was set high above all nations simply by hearkening diligently to the voice of the Lord, as Deuteronomy 28:1 says [4].

Alongside that, the books tell you to seek the blessings themselves, because a blessing counteracts a curse no matter how strong it is [5][7]. You are told to choose life, blessing rather than cursing, as Deuteronomy 30:19 says, and to seek, pray for, and ask for blessings — including the blessing of fruitfulness that God spoke over Adam and Noah in Genesis 1:28 and Genesis 9:1 [5][7]. Being a blessed person is more important than working hard or going to school, for a curse is very effective at neutralizing your hard work and turning your efforts at education into nought [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 23, 24 and 31 of *How To Neutralize Curses*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 1:28; Genesis 3:19; Genesis 9:1; Deuteronomy 28:1; Deuteronomy 30:19; Job 36:11; Isaiah 10:27; Daniel 5:11-12; Matthew 6:33; Romans 8:14 and 1 more.

items.question: How can a young leader make up for not having much experience?
items.text:
The books speak directly to this. A young leader makes up for inexperience by studying history: "The most important subject for a young leader is history," because a young person has to tap into the experiences of others, and his only chance of avoiding certain mistakes is to study those who went before him [1]. History is the greatest source of knowledge and wisdom, second only to the Scriptures, and God even instructed His leaders to teach history so that people would not forget, since forgetting leads to repeating the same mistakes [1]. As Ecclesiastes 1:9,10 says, there is no new thing under the sun [1].

The books also say that some things can only be learned by experience, and that allowing people to go through certain experiences is sometimes the only way to make their minds work in the right way — the Father even trained Jesus this way, for as Hebrews 5:8 says, He "learned obedience by the things which he suffered" [7]. And experience is what teaches the difference between the ideal and the real, making a leader more mature and capable [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 35, 40 and 124 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 1:9-10; Hebrews 5:8.

items.question: Can I get to heaven after I die if I know the right people?
items.book: How to be Born again & Avoid Hell
items.text:
No, friend. When you die you will discover that there is a big gap between heaven and hell, and people cannot cross over from hell to heaven no matter who they are or how much money they had on earth [1][2]. If you want to cross into heaven, you must cross now, because you cannot transfer when you die [1][2]. This will be hard for those used to getting things done through "whom you know," but salvation will be through the blood of Jesus and not through whom you know [1][2].

The rich man in Luke 16 found this out; between him and Abraham a great gulf was fixed, so that no one could pass from one side to the other [1][2]. And unless you are born again, you cannot see the kingdom of God (John 3:3) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 20 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*, chapter 4 of *How to be Born again & Avoid Hell* and chapter 16 of *People Who Went to Hell*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 5:13-14; Luke 16:25-26; John 3:3; John 14:6.
items.label: answerable
cited_books: How to be Born again & Avoid Hell

items.question: Why do people leave the church over small offenses?
items.text:
Our books speak to this. One reason is that people carry unhealed wounds and hurts, and those unresolved hurts cut them off from their church; this is described as one of the commonest reasons for people backsliding and leaving churches [8]. A person may say he was led by the Spirit to leave, yet underneath there was "a slight problem" he could not hide [8].

There is also the matter of shallowness: if you are not deep, you will fall away at the next shaking and crisis, and only a shallow Christian would fall away when a problem arises in the church [5]. And some leave to avoid the confrontations of God's Word rather than admitting their sin and repenting [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Backsliding* and chapter 2 of *How you can become a strong Christian*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 1:10.

items.question: What does it mean that Jesus is a warrior king and we fight alongside him?
items.text:
What a comfort it is that Jesus Himself leads the armies of Heaven and makes war in righteousness — He is called Faithful and True, and the armies of Heaven follow Him on white horses [1][2]. If you want to follow Jesus, you have to join His army and you have to fight [2][6]. He is even a lamb who makes war, and those who are with Him are called, chosen, and faithful [2][4].

So our fighting is never our own — God Himself teaches our hands to war (Psalm 18:34), and we are instructed to fight the good fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12) and to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18) [4]. There is a godly way and a wise way to wage war, and God wants you to wage it in His way and His wisdom [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in *Now We Are At War* and page 1 of *A Good General*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 18:34; 1 Timothy 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:12; Revelation 17:12-14; Revelation 19:11-16.
items.label: answerable

items.question: How can I make my faith stronger?
items.book: Name It Claim It Take It
items.text:
What a good question to ask, and our books speak to it plainly. The principal way to improve your faith is by hearing, for "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Romans 10:17) [2]. The more you listen to preaching and teaching, the more your faith is built up, so keep listening to messages you love over and over, old ones and new ones, and read the books God has placed in your hands [3][5][8].

Faith also grows when you use it; the scripture teaches that we gain by using what we have (Luke 19:15), and your faith grows as you use it [5]. So keep developing your faith, for it is your secret weapon, and you will emerge out of weakness by your faith in God [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Name It Claim It Take It* and chapters 14, 24 and 68 of *Faith Secrets*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 47:9; Luke 19:15; Romans 10:17; 2 Thessalonians 1:3.

items.question: How do we know the Bible is really God's Word and not just written by men?
items.text:
What a good question to ask, and our books speak to it plainly. The Bible itself tells us that "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" (2 Peter 1:20, 21) [3]. So it was written by God through the hands of mortal men — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God" (2 Timothy 3:16) [2][4].

The books also point to the character of the writers: the Bible was written by honest and godly men, because it condemns all sin and even records the sins and faults of its own writers, something evil men would not do [1]. And its heavenly, eternal contents prove it to be of God [1]. The wisest, most godly and honest men acknowledge it as the Word of God; only infidels and ungodly people reject it [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 1 and 7 of *Read your Bible Pray Everyday* and chapter 7 of *Key Facts for New Believers*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 119:9; Psalms 119:105; Acts 20:32; Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:14; 2 Timothy 3:16; Hebrews 1:1-2; Hebrews 2:1-4; 2 Peter 1:20-21.

items.question: What does the Bible say will happen to people who gossip and slander others in the church?
items.text:
The books speak plainly about this. A slanderer is due a curse, and "may a slanderer not endure on the earth; may evil hunt a violent person violently" (Psalm 140:11) — their stay on earth is cut short, and evil hunts them [1]. The Lord asks who may dwell in His tent and settle on His holy hill: the one who "does not slander with his tongue" (Psalm 15:1-3), so a slanderer cannot be allowed to remain in the church or on your leadership team [1]. Scripture even equates disloyalty with blasphemy, and warns that the end of blasphemers and disloyal people will be fire, brimstone, cursing, vexation and desolation of long continuance [5].

The New Testament word for slanderer is *diabolos*, which means devil — "a slanderer is a devil" [8]. And a slanderer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28), causing strife, division and confusion wherever they operate, even separating the sheep from their shepherd [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 5 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty* and chapter 5 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 140:11; Proverbs 16:28; Micah 7:8; Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 3:11; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How can I receive a share of the Holy Spirit's anointing like the seventy elders did with Moses?
items.text:
The Scriptures in our books show that the anointing is shared by God's own hand, not by our effort. It was God who took of the spirit that was upon Moses and put it on the seventy elders — not Moses, and not the elders themselves [3]. So your prayers must be directed to God and not to the anointed man, for "a man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven" (John 3:27) [3].

That said, God has chosen to place His mantle on human beings, and He does not readily introduce a new anointing but shares and passes on what He has already placed on people [5]. So He will direct you to an anointed person, and you must respect and carefully handle that man, for no one ever became anointed by God until he related properly with the anointed person [5]. By involving yourself and joining yourself with people who are anointed, you become anointed too — as Elisha bonded and merged himself with Elijah [2]. And be patient: everyone who received the anointing in the upper room had followed the Lord faithfully for several years [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 2 of *Tasters And Partakers*, chapter 10 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 8 of *Steps to the Anointing*.

Scriptures referenced: Numbers 11:16-17; Numbers 11:24-25; John 3:27; Acts 1:8; Acts 1:21-23; Acts 2:4.

items.question: Why did the people on Malta first think Paul was a murderer and then change their minds to think he was a god?
items.text:
They first judged him by what they saw. When the viper fastened on his hand, the barbarians said among themselves, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live" [2][4]. They expected him to swell up or fall down dead suddenly [3][6].

But when they had looked a great while and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god [2][4][5]. Their thoughts about him shifted from dishonour to honour, and it was after this that Paul prayed and laid hands on Publius' father and healed him, and many others on the island were healed too [4][5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *The Double Mega Missionary Church*, chapter 53 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapters 4 and 8 of *Those Who Honour You*.

Scriptures referenced: Malachi 1:6-8; Acts 27:41-28:10.

items.question: Does sleeping too much really lead to poverty?
items.text:
Yes, our books speak to this plainly. Too much sleep and too much rest lead to poverty: "Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man" (Proverbs 6:9-11) [1]. Poverty comes like a traveller you cannot send away, and want like an armed man you cannot easily dismiss [1]. The same lesson is drawn from the field of the sluggard, overgrown with thorns and nettles (Proverbs 24:30-34) [2][3][5].

King Solomon analysed the problem of poverty around him and concluded that much of it was caused by lack of hard work — that if sleep and folding of arms were dealt with, there would be more prosperity [4]. One book adds the caution that it is not saying all poor people are lazy, but that some stay in poverty because they do not want to work hard [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *Awake, O Sleeper*, chapter 9 of *Why Is This Church Not Working?*, chapter 85 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition* and chapter 11 of *What it means to be as Wise as a Serpent*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 6:9-11; Proverbs 24:30-34.

items.question: A teenager in our youth group says he cuts himself when he is sad.
items.text:
This is a heavy thing to carry, and I'm glad you're asking. Our books speak directly to this. The madman of Gadara, fully under the influence of Satan, cut himself with stones — and Scripture names this self-destruction as a key strategy of demonic attack [2][8]. The passages say plainly that what makes people so sad that they give up on life can only be demons, and that evil spirits may be making a person depressed and sorrowful [3]. They also note that depression is a powerful spirit that can lead people toward suicide, and that self-destruction, suicide and madness are signs of the presence of Lucifer and his delusions [4][5].

So the books would have you take this seriously as a spiritual matter and pray for his deliverance in the name of Jesus [3]. They also observe that people with depression often talk about it first, and that social withdrawal is one of the most telling signs [6]. I would only add what the passages themselves say: receive your deliverance today in the name of Jesus [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 9 and 11 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them*, chapter 2 of *Those who leave you* and chapters 14 and 22 of *Those who are mad*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; 1 Kings 19:2-4; Isaiah 61:3; Ezekiel 28:16-18; Jonah 4:1-9; Mark 5:5; John 16:2; Romans 16:17.

items.question: How can wisdom help me when I'm facing a situation that seems impossible?
items.text:
Wisdom is the application of God's word to impossible situations, and it gives you grace to overcome where others would have drowned [1]. The poor wise man in the besieged city delivered it by wisdom, not by strength, and Scripture says "Wisdom is better than strength" (Ecclesiastes 9:14-16) [1][5]. So when you face something with no way out, wisdom is the key to solving it [4][5].

Wisdom comes through reading and through prayer — read Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and ask God for wisdom, for "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God... and it shall be given him" (James 1:5) [8]. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom, and through wisdom you can overcome impossible situations [3][7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 9 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*, chapter 21 of *Attempt Great Things for God*, chapters 12 and 19 of *Daughter, You Can Make It* and chapter 84 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 4:7-8; Ecclesiastes 9:14-16; Ecclesiastes 10:10; 1 Corinthians 1:24; James 1:5; Wisdom of Solomon 1:1-77.

items.question: How do I understand when Jesus says we must hate our father and mother to be His disciple?
items.text:
This is one of the hard sayings of Jesus, and the books treat it as exactly that: a difficult saying, perhaps too deep for most of us, that you may not be meant to understand but to obey if and when such a day dawns [1][2]. The key is that as you go higher with the Lord, the battle becomes between the good side of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and God's will for your life [2]. Jesus said plainly, "If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple" (Luke 14:26), and in that Scripture He is clearly saying there is a time when such hatred becomes a necessary qualification to be His disciple [2].

The books also say this teaching is reserved for those called at a higher level, applicable to people who may have to hate their wives in order to fulfil their divine calling, and that you receive such explanations by travelling with the anointed rather than only hearing congregational sermons [3]. They note the apparent contradiction with the command to love your wife and to honour your father and mother, and they do not explain it away; they simply hold that there is a place and a time when you must hate your own father and mother in order to please God [1][2]. One book adds that your family will make many sacrifices because of the ministry, and that many do not fulfil God's will because they try to please their wives, since the Bible teaches us to love our wives but to love God first [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 5 of *The Tree and Your Ministry*, chapter 20 of *The Anointed and His Anointing* and chapter 2 of *Losing, Suffering, Sacrificing and Dying*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 2:9; Matthew 13:10-11; Luke 14:1-35; 1 Corinthians 9:15.

items.question: Why doesn't God answer some of my prayers?
items.text:
I hear the ache in that question, and I want to walk through what our books actually say.

Sometimes the answer is no because we are asking for something God is not presently doing. Jesus said, "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do" (John 5:19), and He dealt only with the cases He knew would give positive results [1][2]. So God will have to say "no" when we ask Him for things which are impossible for Him to do [1][2].

Other times, sin is the barrier. "Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you so that He does not hear" (Isaiah 59:1-2) [5]. God does not answer the prayers of disobedient children, but the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much (James 5:16) [7]. Answered prayer is also linked to bearing fruit, for Jesus said the Father gives us whatsoever we ask when we go and bring forth fruit (John 15:16) [7].

And some of it remains a mystery to us. God seems to want us to keep asking the same things, praying without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17), yet He also calls vain repetitions boring, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him (Matthew 6:7-8) [8]. These mysteries must not keep us away from prayer; we keep praying, and we become experienced as we walk with Him [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2 and 9 of *How to Pray*, chapter 5 of *100% Answered Prayer* and chapter 110 of *How You Can Preach Salvation*.

Scriptures referenced: Isaiah 59:1-2; Matthew 6:7-8; John 5:1-8; John 5:19; John 15:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; James 5:16.

These mysteries must not keep us away from prayer; we keep praying, and we become experienced as we walk with Him.

items.question: How can I receive an impartation of understanding from the Holy Spirit?
items.text:
Friend, our books speak to this. The Holy Spirit is the spirit of understanding, and a sudden great illumination of understanding, knowledge or revelation should alert you that an impartation has occurred [1]. One way this comes is by hearing the anointed: when the anointed is speaking, whether in preaching, teaching, or casual conversation, you must be open to receive, for the spirit entered into Ezekiel when he spoke to him (Ezekiel 2:2), and the household of Cornelius received the anointing while Peter was still speaking (Acts 10:44) [2].

So keep listening with faith. You receive the Spirit by the hearing of faith (Galatians 3:2), and hearing with faith makes you receive the anointing [5][8]. It helps to listen more than once, even several times to the same message, soaking it in until you are saturated; keep listening to things you do not understand, and you will suddenly begin to understand them [8]. And pray for the Holy Spirit, for He is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and the wisdom of God is taught by the Holy Spirit [3][6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 11 of *The Anointed and His Anointing*, chapter 31 of *The Sweet Influences of the Anointing*, chapter 13 of *Seeing And Hearing* and chapter 32 of *Wisdom Is the Principle Thing For Your Minsitry*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 25:14; Isaiah 11:1; Ezekiel 2:2; Luke 11:13; Acts 10:44; 1 Corinthians 2:8; Galatians 3:2; Ephesians 6:12; 1 Timothy 5:22.

items.question: What happens if I don't forgive someone?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak plainly about this, and it is sobering. They say God will not forgive your sins and will not hear your prayers if you do not forgive others [1][2], and that the Lord was angry with the servant who would not forgive, handing him over to the tormentors [1][2]. Those tormentors can touch you with sickness, disease, poverty, and marital disharmony [2]. As Matthew 18:32-35 says, so shall your heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses [2].

The books also warn that unforgiveness left unchecked becomes bitterness, and bitterness can spread until a person hates all men, withdraws, and lives alone [7][5]. One passage goes so far as to say unforgiveness is one sin God will not forgive, and that it may be for you the difference between life and death [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3, 4, 5 and 7 of *Forgiveness Made Easy 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: Genesis 46:26-27; Genesis 48:20-22; Psalms 130:4; Jeremiah 17:9; Matthew 18:32-35; Mark 11:25.

items.question: What is blasphemy?
items.text:
Blasphemy is speaking reproachfully about God and His work — speaking impiously or irreverently about God, His church, and His servants, attacking their good reputation with malicious and injurious words [1]. It is also defined as an act of cursing or reviling God, and the books go so far as to equate disloyalty with blasphemy, since to God disloyalty is a form of blasphemy [2]. It includes vilification, slander, and injurious speech spoken against another's good name [3].

The books also warn that it is not only unbelievers who blaspheme; born-again Christians can too, because blasphemy is not only speaking irreverently against God but also speaking irreverently about sacred things, and ministers of the gospel are in a certain sense sacred, having been set apart to minister the holy things of the Lord [6]. So accusing a minister of being a false prophet, a deceiver, anointed of the devil, or the like, when all you have heard is a rumour or a publication of half-truths, could be blaspheming [6].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *Those Who Make Shipwreck*, chapter 9 of *Pillars of Loyalty*, chapter 16 of *Victory Secrets* and chapter 6 of *Poison: Taming The Tongue*.

Scriptures referenced: Mark 3:28-30; Revelation 2:9; Revelation 13:4-7.

items.question: How does the blood of Jesus cleanse me from my sins?
items.text:
The books say plainly that nothing else can do it — not soap, not orange juice, not any other name. Only the blood of Jesus has the power to wash away the stain of our sins, our lies, our stealing, our fornication and our murders [1][2]. As Acts 4:12 says, there is salvation in no other, for there is none other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved [1][5].

Scripture puts it this way: "the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin" (1 John 1:7), and "if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9) [3][7]. The books describe the blood as a sin-removing liquid, carrying away our sin and filthiness the way blood carries away carbon dioxide [7], and they picture it as a two-step work: you are forgiven, and then you are cleansed, because even after forgiveness there is often a scent of the past evils that contaminate us [4][6][8]. As Revelation 1:5 says, he "washed us from our sins in his own blood" [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12, 13, 14, 16 and 46 of *How You Can Preach Salvation* and chapters 3, 5 and 6 of *Blood Power*.

Scriptures referenced: Zechariah 3:3-4; John 6:54-55; Acts 4:12; 1 John 1:7; 1 John 1:9; Revelation 1:5; Revelation 22:11.

items.question: Does God want me to fight spiritual battles, and how do I do that?
items.text:
Yes, friend, the books are clear that God does want you to fight. Jesus Christ leads the armies of heaven and makes war in righteousness (Revelation 19:11), and if you want to follow Jesus, you have to join His army and fight [3]. Anyone who thinks we are not at war lacks understanding; God's Word says we are to war a good warfare and fight a good fight [3]. As a minister, you have even more enemies and need to know how to overcome them [3].

As for how, you must accept that you will build for God and fight many battles at the same time — fighting battles outside and within, physical beings and spiritual beings, enemies who look like enemies and enemies who look like friends [1]. Nehemiah's builders each worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other, sword girded at his side as he built (Nehemiah 4:17-18) [1]. You must also put on the whole armour of God to stand against the wiles of the devil (Ephesians 6:11), for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds (2 Corinthians 10:4) [6]. And remember that our principal enemy is Satan, not other human beings [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 13 of *The Art of Following*, chapters 1 and 60 of *A Good General* and chapter 4 of *Transform Your Pastoral Ministry*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 4:17-18; 2 Corinthians 10:4; Ephesians 6:11; Revelation 19:11; Revelation 20:1-3; Revelation 20:10.

items.question: Do pastors and church workers have the right to be paid and take time off?
items.book: Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)
items.text:
Yes, dear pastor, the books speak plainly to both. On pay: a full-time church worker should be considered for emoluments, benefits, accommodation, transportation, medical care, insurance and the like when the organisation is capable [4], and "they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel" (1 Corinthians 9:14) [8]. Paul asks, "What soldier in the army has to pay his own expenses?" and reminds us that God's law says not to muzzle the ox treading out the wheat (1 Corinthians 9:6-9) [2]. A lay pastor or volunteer, though, must not be paid any form of remuneration; anything given to them is a gift, not a salary [7].

On rest: rest is part of God's plan for His cherished ministers, and vacations, days off and times of rest are their right [1]. Paul asks, "Or do only Barnabas and I not have a right to refrain from working?" (1 Corinthians 9:6) [1], and full-time workers should have rest and leave periods, with the kinds of leave determined by the administrators and bishops [3][4]. Mondays can be taken as a day of rest and a day off [3]. One caution: in emergencies affecting the church or nation, all full-time church workers must cancel vacations and return to work [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Rules of Full Time Ministry (2nd edition)*, chapters 5 and 55 of *The Gift Of Governments* and chapter 38 of *The Art of Leadership - 3rd Edition*.

Scriptures referenced: 1 Samuel 15:22-23; Ecclesiastes 10:7; 1 Corinthians 9:4; 1 Corinthians 9:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 1 Timothy 4:15; 2 Timothy 2:6.

items.question: How do I heal from the hurts and offenses I've experienced in life and ministry?
items.text:
Friend, the books speak directly to this. First, expect that wounds will come — if you are in ministry, expect to be hurt and wounded by fellow pastors; if you are married, expect to be wounded by your spouse [2]. Offences must come, as Matthew 18:6-7 says [2][5]. So the question is not whether you'll be hurt, but how you come out of it.

Confess your faults one to another and pray for one another, that you may be healed, as James 5:16 says [2][5]. Your broken heart must be healed; you are healed when you are no longer bitter [2]. The Lord Himself was anointed to heal the brokenhearted and set at liberty them that are bruised, as Luke 4:18-19 says [2]. And you are to come out of your tests with patience — cheerful, hopeful endurance — as James 1:4 makes clear [2].

Do not let the hurt isolate you. When people separate themselves from other Christians to avoid being hurt again, that separation leads to total isolation from the body of Christ and a weakening of their Christian life [1][3]. The author himself decided at one point to stay away from people, then realized he was being cut off from the rest of the church because of unhealed wounds, and chose to let the wounds heal [1]. Press on toward healing and wholeness; hold to Romans 8:28, that all things work together for good to them that love the Lord [4]. Your wounds will become scars, and the scars will be the basis of your healing ministry — without scars you will never have authority [4]. Jesus was wounded many times but He forgave, and that is the example we must follow [8].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 17 of *TS2. Hope Secrets*, chapter 3 of *Backsliding*, chapter 9 of *Those Who Are Offended* and chapter 8 of *Those who are Dangerous Sons*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 21:18-23; Matthew 18:6-7; Luke 4:18-19; Romans 8:28; James 1:4; James 5:16.

items.question: How should an assistant minister behave during counselling sessions with the senior pastor?
items.text:
During counselling sessions, an assisting minister must not contribute any counsel that is contrary to what is being said, and must not try to develop a completely new train of thought, which may only confuse the one receiving counsel [1][2]. Do not try to impress anyone with some "high-sounding" wisdom; simply help your senior to say what he is saying better and emphasize what he has already said [1][2].

Do not remain quiet during counselling sessions, as this will only make you look like a spectator and will make the counsellee feel awkward [1][2]. You can use simple but powerful phrases at intervals, such as "Do you understand what Pastor is saying?", "Do you understand that Pastor is only trying to help you?", "Pastor is only saying this because he loves you," and "I wish I had had someone speak to me this way when I was in a similar situation" [2][3]. As you interject comments like these, you lend a greater impact to his words [2][3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 7 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 3 of *Ministerial Ethics*.

Scriptures referenced: Proverbs 18:16.

items.question: What should I do if I'm bitter about being moved away from a pastor who helped me?
items.text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Our books speak to this, and gently.

Bitterness is an advanced, deep-seated form of offense, and many who walk out of a church are offended Christians who became bitter, with wounds that never healed [2]. The warning is real: "Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled" (Hebrews 12:15) [2][3]. You are liberated from bitterness as you forgive, and it is possible for you to forgive — allow the Holy Spirit to help you; as Mark 11:25 says, when you stand praying, forgive if you have anything against any [8].

It also helps to talk about your pain with spiritually mature counsellors, your pastors or godly friends, and to receive God's love, replacing feelings of rejection with confidence in His Word [8]. And be careful not to let this colour the rest of your ministry — a lack of trust reveals continuing bitterness in you [3].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 4 of *How you can become a strong Christian*, chapter 10 of *Those who leave you* and chapter 59 of *Model Marriage*.

Scriptures referenced: Psalms 103:8; Mark 11:24-25; Hebrews 12:15; James 5:16.

items.question: How does prayer make me stronger?
items.text:
Prayer is where your strength comes from, pastor. When you cry out to God, He answers and strengthens you with strength in your soul (Psalm 138:3) [2]. Every time you pray, your spirit is strengthened [3], and praying in tongues builds you up and makes you stronger, for "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4) [1].

That strength is what carries you in ministry and in battle. Through prayer you receive strength to survive the attacks of the enemy, and the Lord stands with you and delivers you out of the mouth of the lion (2 Timothy 4:17) [2]. Prayer also gives you emotional strength, steadying your soul when your feelings would pull you the wrong way [2]. And it is the source of your great strength, the very thing the enemy targets, for prayer is the key to rising above human abilities (Judges 16:4-6) [4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 12 and 14 of *Pr 6. Prayer Opportunities* and chapter 2 of *Prayer Changes Things*.

Scriptures referenced: Judges 16:4-6; Psalms 138:3; Matthew 26:41; Luke 22:41-43; 1 Corinthians 14:4; Ephesians 3:14-19; 1 Timothy 1:12; 2 Timothy 1:6-7; 2 Timothy 4:17.

items.question: How do I deal with demonic attacks on my family?
items.book: Demons and How to Deal with Them
items.text:
Our books speak to this. Attacks that involve stealing, killing and destruction are caused by the devil and his agents, and spending time to bind demonic powers and destroy their plans will protect you from such evil attacks [1]. When you deal with thieves, murderers and destroyers you are dealing with Satan himself, so deal with the devil in your life by dealing properly with them [1].

It also helps to identify what you are facing, for demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to deal with them; specifically mentioning the name of the problem and dealing with it is the key to dealing with demonic powers, which is why Jesus asked the madman of Gadara, "What is thy name?" (Luke 8:30) [4]. Persistent attacks on your family, life and health, like Job's, are a sign of demonic activity, and Job's troubles came from Satan's direct attack on him, as Job 1:12 shows [5]. You can also tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, and emphasizing salvation all tighten the security of your spirit man against demons, as Ephesians 6:14 says [7].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 18 of *One of You is a Devil*, chapter 20 of *Demons and How to Deal with Them* and chapters 5 and 24 of *Know Your Invisible Enemies*.

Scriptures referenced: Job 1:12; Mark 5:3; Mark 5:5; Luke 8:30; John 10:10; Ephesians 6:14.

When you deal with thieves, murderers and destroyers you are dealing with Satan himself, so deal with the devil in your life by dealing properly with them.

It also helps to identify what you are facing, for demons and demonic activity must be identified in order to deal with them; specifically mentioning the name of the problem and dealing with it is the key to dealing with demonic powers, which is why Jesus asked the madman of Gadara, "What is thy name?" (Luke 8:30).
Persistent attacks on your family, life and health, like Job's, are a sign of demonic activity, and Job's troubles came from Satan's direct attack on him, as Job 1:12 shows.

You can also tighten your security: staying with the truth and avoiding deception, practicing righteousness and avoiding sin, and emphasizing salvation all tighten the security of your spirit man against demons, as Ephesians 6:14 says.

items.question: Can someone who gossips or slanders others still be a member of our church?
items.text:
Our books speak plainly to this. A slanderer will not be allowed to remain in the church: Psalm 15 describes those who may dwell in God's holy hill, and it says the one who does not slander with his tongue is the one who may stay [1]. Once you have slandered the brethren, you can no longer be allowed to stay and dwell amongst us [1][2]. The instruction is to drive away slanderers, let them go, and not to feel sorry for them [2]. A slanderer is a living, moving, active human devil in your midst [6].

So do not receive people who come with stories and rumours against their former church, or who are filled with unverifiable, wicked stories about their last employer [2]. And be careful not to be fooled by those who seem to bring news of the downfall of your competitors and brothers, for the downfall of your brother does not mean you will do well [2].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 9 of *Those Who Are Slanderers*.

Scriptures referenced: Leviticus 19:16; Psalms 15:1-5; Psalms 54:5; Psalms 140:11.

items.question: Why is loyalty so important in ministry, especially during hard times?
items.text:
Loyalty matters because it is the principal qualification for every minister — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2) [3][7]. It is not gifting, friendliness, or oratory that qualifies a person, but faithfulness and loyalty [3][7].

Hard times are where loyalty shows its true worth: in the good times everybody seems loyal, but loyalty is most appreciated in hard times [1][2]. Jesus told His disciples they would receive a special reward because they had continued with Him in His temptations (Luke 22:28-29), and their names are written on the foundations of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14) [1][2][4]. Those who stick with you through difficult times are different from those who come in when everything is working well [2][4].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 3 and 7 of *Why Loyalty?* and chapter 1 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty*.

Scriptures referenced: Ecclesiastes 12:12; Matthew 25:21; Luke 22:28-29; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Revelation 21:14.

items.question: How does the Holy Spirit teach us today?
items.text:
The Holy Spirit teaches us first and foremost as a teacher — that is His number one manifestation, the way He makes Himself visible and relevant to us [3]. Jesus promised the Comforter who "shall teach you all things" (John 14:26), and the principal work of the Spirit is to guide us into all truth [3][4]. So when you read your Bible and deep revelation of the Word opens up to you, the Holy Spirit is being manifest [3].

He teaches in several ways: through anointed teachers of the Word, so don't miss His voice coming to you through them [5]; by guiding you toward truth, which is toward Jesus Himself [5]; by pointing you to certain books you should read [5]; by reminding you of what Jesus has said in His Word (John 14:26) [8]; and by giving you knowledge, since God has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness through the knowledge of Him (2 Peter 1:3) [8]. He also teaches through revelation — sudden bursts of insight — and He will show you things to come (John 16:13) [1].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 8 of *The Love of the Spirit* and chapter 7 of *Amplify Your Ministry with Miracles And Manifestations Of The Holy Spirit*.

Scriptures referenced: Nehemiah 9:20; John 8:32; John 14:26; John 16:12-14; Ephesians 1:17; 2 Peter 1:3; Revelation 10:8.

items.question: How can I tell when someone in my team is becoming disloyal?
items.text:
Friend, the books say disloyalty doesn't happen overnight—it's a process, and most people don't even notice it in themselves or in those they work with [1]. The first stage is an independent spirit: someone still part of the church but doing what he wants in spite of contrary instructions, obeying only the instructions he thinks are important [1].

Watch too for the signs: people who absent themselves when the church is going through hard times, since it's in times of pressure that you see a person's true character [2]. Inflexibility is another manifestation—stubborn, defiant, unwilling to go beyond what's stipulated, not prepared to adapt, and not willing to take correction when confronted, as Saul argued with Samuel [3]. And among assistants, be alert to the one who says "I knew all along this would not work," or who has no comment at all when you bring a new idea or vision [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapters 2, 5 and 8 of *Loyalty and Disloyalty* and chapter 7 of *Those Who Are Ignorant*.

Scriptures referenced: John 7:5.

items.question: What should I read during it?
items.book: How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day
items.text:
The books give a few ways to choose your reading. You can choose a book of the Bible and read a few verses every day, always remembering where you ended so you continue from the same place the next day — the author mentions having wonderful quiet times reading through Luke and Ephesians in the New Testament, and Genesis and 1st and 2nd Samuel in the Old [5]. Or you can choose a personality from the Bible and follow their life story, a few verses at a time, such as passages about Moses [5].

You may also refer to your daily Bible reading guide, since these are very helpful in developing a regular quiet time habit and you will benefit from anointed teachers whose ministry will help you grow [4][6]. And read expecting God to speak to you, as Psalm 119:18 says, "Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law" [5].

Bishop Dag Heward-Mills talks about this in chapter 3 of *The Secret*, chapter 8 of *Key Facts for New Believers* and chapter 11 of *How You Can Have an Effective Quiet Time with God Every Day*.
